citations.text: There were four transhipment consignments of products during 2015 which were destined for the Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP. This BIP had not detected the relevant TRACES notification sent from the first EU BIP although staff stated that TRACES notifications are checked twice per day. The competent authority contacted Customs who confirmed that all four consignments had been released for free circulation as they had CVEDs (see finding 10). A similar finding was reported in report DG(SANTE) 2014-7012 but corrective actions have not been implemented. Conclusions on the system to ensure presentation of consignments for veterinary checks

There is a system is in place to ensure that no consignment from a non-EU country is introduced into EU territory without being subjected to veterinary checks, although the system did not work for consignments transhipped via other Member States during 2015 at Budapest-Liszt Ferenc BIP. 5.3.2 Veterinary checks and the decision on the consignment Legal requirements Articles 4, 8, 15 and Annex III of Directive 97/78/EC, Article 4(1) of Directive 91/496/EEC, Article 27(2) of Commission Regulation 142/2011, 4(2)(d) of Commission Decision 2001/812/EC, Annex II of Commission Decision 97/794/EC and Commission Decision 94/360. recommendations.text: To ensure that physical checks carried out at BIPs are in line with the requirements of Article 4(2)(d) of Decision 2001/812/EC and Annex III of Directive 97/78/EC.

citations.text: In relation to the implementation of physical checks on consignments (products), the audit team noted that: Röszke BIP received 82% of consignments presented at Hungarian BIPs in 2014. Staff at Röszke BIP stated that physical checks are often carried out without unloading any of the consignment from the means of transport and can be based on only a visual examination of the boxes. This approach does not comply with the requirements of Section 3.4 of the BIP Manual. It also does not comply with Annex III of Directive 97/78/EC which describes the aim and types of physical checks to be conducted at BIPs. This also means that CVEDs do not reflect the reality of the controls done at the BIPs. Finding 22 from report DG SANCO/2014-7008 reported on the lack of unloading for physical checks at Röszke BIP and the situation has not changed. Contrary to the requirements of Decision 94/360/EC Röszke BIP does not implement the reduced physical checks regime. The excessive number of controls is not based on suspicion or a documented risk assessment. The BIP implemented physical checks in 905 out of 1,237 consignments destined for import during 2014.

In general, veterinary checks and decisions on consignments are correct but there are several issues which undermine the effectiveness of the system. The most significant of these is at Röszke BIP where the system to implement physical checks does not comply with national or EU requirements. Appropriate corrective action was not implemented in response to a related finding in report DG(SANCO) 2014-7008. This means that CVEDs do not reflect the reality of the controls done at the BIPs and the competent authority does not ensure that corrective action is taken when needed.

responses.response: The requirements for physical checks in Point 3.4 of the BIP al has been modified accordingly and the 2nd point of the Letter also includes some proposal on the practical implementing.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when confirmation of receipt/exit for relevant consignments is not received by the entry BIP within the legally applicable deadline, appropriate follow-up is implemented as required by Articles 8, 11 and 15 of Directive 97/78/EC.

citations.text: Only Röszke BIP has received incoming transit consignments in recent years, e.g. 628 consignments during 2014. Details on non-confirmed consignments were sent about every two months to the central competent authority for further investigation. The audit team noted that the BIP did not consult with local Customs before consulting the central competent authority. This is not in line with internal procedures and causes unnecessary delays. It was clarified during the audit that the central office was not aware that Röszke BIP had not been contacting local Customs before it forwarded the list to them.
At Záhony BIP 20 out of 21 consignments were checked in 2014. In Röszke 4 out of 13 consignments were checked during 2014. Neither BIP followed-up the consignments not presented for checks.

There was one consignment in TRACES which indicated Eperjeske as the exit BIP (notified in December 2013). The BIP had not detected the notification via their daily screening and therefore had not informed Customs. The CVED indicated that the consignment was being transported by road. The competent authority confirmed that it had exited via BIP Záhony without being checked by the BIP. The same staff is responsible for import controls at the BIPs Eperjeske and Záhony, yet the consignment had not been detected. Transits of live animals

There were no entry transits and only four exit transits via Hungarian BIPs during 2014 and 2015. No Part IIIs of the CVEDs were completed by the exit BIPs in TRACES. One 11 consignment was discussed during the audit, i.e. a cat which entered via Budapest-Liszt Ferenc and with Röszke as the exit BIP. The animal was destined for Serbia and the CVED did not contain any details for the means of transport after the entry BIP and therefore the exit BIP could not detect it. Budapest-Liszt Ferenc did not receive any confirmation of exit via TRACES and did not follow this up with Customs. Controls on free and customs warehouses

Veterinary checks carried out at entry BIPs on consignments in transit comply with EU requirements and ensure that only eligible consignments are accepted. The system to promptly identify and follow-up consignments for which no confirmation of receipt at destination has been received by the entry BIP was not being implemented as planned, reducing the ability of the system to identify non-conforming consignments that have not left the Union as planned.

responses.response: The BIP officer's attention has been drawn to the procedure already described in the BIP Manual with point 9 of the Letter.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all BIPs comply with the approval requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC and Directive 91/496/EEC including cleaning/disinfection and calibration of equipment.

citations.text: Eperjeske BIP Facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions are compliant with the exception of: Facilities are shared for checks on consignments destined for human and non-human consumption but there is no documented risk assessment contrary to Article 4(5) of Decision 2001/812/EC. There is currently no system to ensure that equipment is calibrated as required. 12

Kelebia BIP Facilities and equipment were found to be sub-standard due to their poor maintenance (in addition to the main deficiencies identified in the other BIPs, at Kelebia, the most serious included broken doors preventing access to the unloading area) and hygiene conditions were poor.

Röszke BIP Facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions are compliant with the exception of: The storage room for frozen consignments destined for human consumption was being used to store paper files and office equipment at the time of the audit and was therefore unavailable for its intended use. The BIP staff stated that this situation had existed for about one year and no specific deadline for resolution was available. Although a written procedure exists to ensure appropriate cleaning and disinfection of the entire BIP, no records were available of its implementation. There is currently no effective system to ensure that equipment is calibrated as required.

Záhony BIP Facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions are compliant with the exception of: There is currently no system to ensure that relevant equipment is calibrated as required. Conclusions on the compliance of the facilities, equipment and hygiene conditions of the BIPs visited

BIPs have been constructed to an adequate standard but the lack of maintenance limits the possibility to use the facilities for their intended purposes and/or implement official controls correctly. Specifically in Kelebia BIP the facilities cannot be used for identity and physical checks.

responses.response: The requirement for a local supervision of cleaning/disinfection, calibration of devices, etc. have been set up in a new Annex in the BIP Manual (Annex XX). The BIP officer's attention has been drawn to this requirement in point 8 and 10 of the Letter. Page: 1 ort ref. recommendations.text: Ensure that adequate un-announced official controls are carried out, based on documented procedures, on vaccine bait storage before and during vaccine distribution to verify the maintenance of the cold chain and that the vaccine quality is maintained until distribution. Articles 3(2) and 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: There are no documented procedures containing information and instructions for officials carrying out inter alia controls on storage conditions, transport and handling of vaccine baits1. Such procedures are required under Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and are aimed at ensuring the quality and consistency of official controls that is required under Article 4(4) of the Regulation. Conclusions on competent authorities

Although training on rabies eradication and surveillance takes place at all relevant levels, the lack of documented procedures for official controls by official veterinarians on the storage of oral rabies vaccine may lead to inconsistencies in the implementation of these controls.

Article 3(2) Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 states that official controls shall be carried out without prior warning. However, all controls on storage conditions, transport and distribution of the oral rabies vaccine carried out by the competent authorities are pre-announced to the operators. Before the start of each campaign Circular letters are sent from NFCSO to the Food Chain Safety and Animal Health Directorates of County Government Office, comprising inter alia the schedule and area of the campaign, information on vaccine storage/ distribution and instructions to carry out an official control at each airfield during the vaccine distribution. For the autumn campaign 2014 this circular letter was issued three weeks before the start of the campaign and indicated suitable days for visits by official veterinarians to each airfield and contact details for agreeing the date and time for the visit with the subcontractors. 8 Visits to each airfield by NFCSO-VMPD were pre-announced to the subcontractor and dates for these visits were indicated in the contractor's plan for the 2014 autumn campaign.

Once the 2014 vaccine batches had been accepted into the cold store the responsibility for maintaining the cold chain was delegated to the contractor/subcontractors and not closely verified by the competent authorities. The contractor for aerial bait distribution had delegated the responsibility for ensuring that the cold chain was maintained from acceptance of the vaccine batches at the cold store until the end of the vaccination campaign 3-4 weeks to several subcontractors. o In one airfield the subcontractor (flight operator) had the day-to-day responsibilities for correct storage of the vaccine consignment, transport of vaccine baits to the airfield, storage there, batch traceability, aerial distribution of baits and manual distribution to subcontractors. o Two other subcontractors were responsible for transporting the vaccine from the cold store and storage at all the other airfields in the refrigerated trucks used for the transport. o One subcontractor was responsible for manual distribution of vaccine baits. NFCSO-VMPD had planned to carry out one announced visit to each airfield during each distribution period. Records from the 2014 autumn campaign showed that such visits (by staff from central level) had been made to five of the six airfields. The NFCSO-VMPD visits were recorded on standardised check lists and had been made in the presence of the operator and sometimes the official veterinarian. The check list includes checks on records of vaccine stock, manually kept temperature records, storage temperature at the time of the visit, the functionality of planes and bait drop equipment, and the texture of vaccine baits. The NFCSO-VMPD visits did not include checks on flight route data or bait drop data at the airfield and neither the NFCSO nor the contractor could cross-check the manual temperature records against the built-in temperature recording devices in the transport/storage vehicles as they had no access to the readings of these during the campaign. In the Circular letter for the 2014 autumn campaign District Offices were instructed to carry out one announced inspection on each airfield during the distribution period. Records from the 2014 autumn campaign showed that four of the six airfields had not been inspected from District Offices.

The procedures agreed between the competent authority and the contractor for immediate reporting of non-compliant storage temperatures were not adhered to in 2014. The contractor for vaccine distribution does not carry out any checks on the activities of the subcontractors during the vaccine storage period or during vaccine distribution. However, the subcontractors are instructed to contact the contractor in case of problems. NFCSO-VMPD stated that it had been agreed with the contractor that such contacts should be made if the storage temperatures exceeded -15oC and records of such interventions should be provided in the final report from the campaign. Records in the final report from the 2014 autumn campaign showed no evidence of contacts between the subcontractor and the contractor when storage temperatures had exceeded -15oC for 4 days in two of the airfields. In the second of these airfields storage temperatures up to -5oC were recorded. Further checks showed that these problems had concerned one transport vehicle which, although a malfunctioning cooling unit had been identified by the flight subcontractor at one airfield, had subsequently been used by the transport subcontractor for storing vaccine at a second airfield. The contractor stated that 9 the subcontractor for vaccine transport and airfield storage would be requested not to use this vehicle in the next vaccination campaign. No deviating results in population immunity for 2014 were seen in in the areas serviced by the two airfields where non-compliant storage temperatures had been recorded however the monitoring results cover the whole year.

Once the vaccine has been accepted upon delivery to the cold store the responsibility for the implementation of an oral vaccination campaign rests with private operators (subcontractors) who are neither supervised by the main contractor nor subject to unannounced official controls by competent authorities during the campaign. This system is not effective as illustrated by the fact that deficiencies in the cold chain during 2014 had neither been corrected by the contractor nor reported at the time to the competent authorities.

responses.response: The official control of storage of the vaccines in the cold store before distribution is the task of the district official veterinarian. Additionally, as of 2015 spring campaign an un-announced control of storage conditions in the cold store performed by the CA has been introduced. The storage conditions during distribution are controlled at the airfields by the competent district official veterinarian. To harmonize these field controls, a check- list has been issued by the CA before 2015 spring campaign.

recommendations.text: Ensure better coordination and cooperation within the CCA, as required by Article 4(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, with a view to including producers of seed for sprouting in the scope of official controls.

citations.text: During official controls at sprouts and packer establishments, the CAs can gather information about suppliers of seeds, in particular through verification of traceability. The audit team noted that following such checks, CGO DFCSAHU had identified a number of producers of seeds for sprouting (see paragraphs 60, 65, 70 and 71). Based on the statement that the responsible divisions of NFCSO DPPSC and CGO DFCSPPSC/DFCSA were not aware of the existence of such producers, the audit team noted that the information had not been shared between the various bodies concerned resulting in such producers not being subject to official controls. This limited cooperation does not fulfil the requirements of Article 4(5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusion on Designation of CAs and Resources for Official Controls

The CAs in the context of this audit are designated at all stages of primary production as required by Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and this gives a good basis for the implementation of official controls. However, limited coordination and cooperation between the government bodies involved results in some producers of seeds for sprouting not being subject to official controls. 6 5.2.2 Registration / Approval of Food Establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/204, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings Registration of Food Establishments

In this establishment a number of different seeds are sprouted. As part of the official control the inspector reviewed the label information for the different types of seeds held in storage. The inspector informed the audit team that in this FBO, all seeds for sprouting were of EU origin. Moreover, a variety of seeds for sprouting was from a Hungarian producer.
The audit team noted that evidence of seeds for sprouting produced in Hungary, although already outlined in the previous inspection report, did not result in appropriate actions from the CAs. 12

The inspector started the traceability verification from three 200g packs of seeds for sprouting: radish, sunflower and rape seeds labelled as "Agriculture EU". The inspector correctly asked for evidence of origin and for the declaration of "seeds for sprouting" on the invoice documentation. The sunflower seeds for sprouting were from a Hungarian producer.
The CCA confirmed that being not aware of any Hungarian producers of seeds for sprouting, these producers are not controlled as such (see paragraph 15 and 48).

The guide will be a balance of information provided by CGO DFCSPPSC/DFCSA DIVISION FOR FOOD SAFETY, QUALITY AND CONTROL and CGO DFCSAHU and CGO DIVISION FOR PLANT PROTECTION AND SOIL CONSERVATION. Deadline: end of 2017

recommendations.text: Ensure, as required by Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, that official controls consistently enforce the requirements laid down by Annex I, Chapter 3.3, Part A.1 and Part A.2 of the said Regulation (as regards preliminary testing of seeds intended for sprouting and sprouts).

citations.text: The inspector verified the sampling plan of the FBO, specifically the results of the preliminary tests for seeds for sprouting and the tests of final products (sprouts). Seeds for sprouts are not tested before use (preliminary tests). The CAs allowed the FBO to use, instead of preliminary tests for seeds, the analytical reports on the seeds provided by the supplier. Moreover, the tests of the final products (sprouts) were available, but the frequency was not respected and samples were not analysed for STEC. In the previous reports there was no evidence of non-compliances regarding analytical frequency and parameters. The inspector informed the audit team that she was aware from previous inspections that the FBO did not comply with the requirements laid down by Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of the Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. However, on the basis that this could have impacted the economic situation of the FBO, the inspector stated that no actions had been requested in order to resolve this non-compliance.

The CAs confirmed that this second sprout-producing establishment (not visited) complied with the frequency for preliminary tests on seeds for sprouting and final tests on sprouts. However, STEC was not tested as required by Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of the Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The CAs informed the audit team that the inspector of this second facility was aware from previous inspections that also this FBO did not comply with the requirements laid down by Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of the Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. However, the high price and the limited availability of STEC analyses was the reason for not requiring this.

The inspector verified the sampling plan of the FBO, specifically the results of the preliminary tests on seeds for sprouting and the tests on final products (sprouts). Seeds for sprouting were regularly tested according to Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 before growing. All the results were compliant. The tests of the final products (sprouts) were available and the frequency had been respected. However, samples of final product were not analysed for STEC. This non-compliance had been identified in previous inspection reports and a deadline (not yet expired at the time of the audit) had been given to the operator to address the situation.

Official controls at sprout-producing establishments, contrary to what is required by Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, do not consistently enforce the requirements laid down in Annex I, Chapter 3.3 of the said Regulation (as regards preliminary testing of seeds intended for sprouting and sprouts). Enforcement of such requirements had only been initiated recently in the establishments visited.

responses.response: on (EC) No 2073/2005, NFCSO FFSD will develop a guide for the official control of the requirements laid sprouting establishments covering the requirements of art A.2 of the said Regulation (EC) 2073/2005. The guide will set out the f seeds intended for procedure to be followed by the official controllers recording how the FBOs meet the requirements of the regulation as preliminary testing of seeds intended for sprouting and sprouts. The guide will contain the procedure to be followed in the case of non-compliance. Deadline: end of 2017 Page: 1

recommendations.text: Ensure that supervision carried out by the CCA is adequate in order to 2. guarantee that controls carried out by CBs are effective, as required by 3. Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, and in particular that: The scope of the supervision covers the operational performance of the CBs, as required by Article 92c of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; CBs immediately notify the CAs when the results of controls indicate non-compliance or point to the likelihood of non- compliance, as required by Article 27(5)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007; When non-compliances are detected by the CCA in the performance of CBs, reports are submitted with no undue delay, to allow the CBs to take corrective actions in a timely manner. This recommendation is based upon conclusions No 24 and 25 Ensure that there is a system in place for the verification of the exemption of retailers in line with Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 10(2) of the Ministerial Decree. This recommendation is based upon conclusion No 34 Ensure that, when the control arrangements are first implemented, CBs verify the completeness of the declaration submitted by operators, as 29 required by Articles 63(1) and (2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. This recommendation is based upon conclusion No 35 4. Ensure that CBs receive all necessary information from operators in due time before the inspections, and in particular that: The schedule of the production of crops is submitted before a date indicated by CBs, as required by Article 71 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008; Any change in the measures referred to in Article 63 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 is notified by operators and adequately assessed by CBs; Information submitted by operators concerning quantities harvested and yield estimations is verified by CBs, in order to ensure an adequate verification of the balance between input and output required by Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The recommendation is based upon conclusion No 45 5. Ensure that risk analysis carried out by CBs to select operators for additional controls is in line with Article 65(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, and in particular that quantities produced are taken into account. The recommendation is based upon conclusion No 46 6. Ensure that the selection of operators for additional controls is based on the results of the risk analysis carried out by CBs, and that at least 10% of all inspections are carried out unannounced, as required by Article 92c(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that officials at district level have the competence to carry out effective controls, as requested by NÉBIH, and in accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and should consider in doing so, the reasons why NÉBIH directed follow up-action and training have not been able to address previous DG SA s since 2011, and put in place suitable measures to address the root causes.

citations.text: The County offices provide training for district offices mainly on certification of animals but also on welfare issues. During 2016 NÉBIH required all counties to give training on animal welfare requirements to those district official veterinarians dispatching consignments for long journeys. NÉBIH supplied training materials (including the elements in paragraph 3 a-g above) and all officials were trained by December 2016.

Most officials at district level did not take into account the training or instructions regarding the time taken to cross the border at Turkey and the working hours of Turkish veterinary authorities there, in their verification of journey log planning (see paragraphs 26 to 28 below). This resulted in incorrect journey planning and animals subjected to routinely longer journey times.

Staff at district level generally did not know how to check certain requirements requested by NÉBIH, e.g. approving vehicle deck surface areas and suitability of drinkers or analysis of retrospective satellite navigation system or temperature records from long journeys (see paragraphs 10, 11, 12, 26 27 and 28 below). This is despite training and guidance from both central and county level. This lack of knowledge or competence in carrying out tasks at district level is not in compliance with Article 6 of Regulation 882/2004.

There has been inadequate progress in rectifying the deficiencies reported during the Commission audit to Hungary DG(SANCO) 2011/6045 on animal welfare during transport. Actions taken by the Hungarian authorities to rectify the deficiencies were ineffective as the same deficiencies were found at district level in 2017.

Official controls at district level do not ensure transporter's compliance. This together with the absence of verification in a number of key areas might cause unnecessary pain or suffering to animals during long distance transport by road to non-EU countries.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that the current system for approving means of transport for long distances includes: proper guidance and assessment of the suitability of vehicles' drinking systems for different types of animals and different categories of those types, as required by Annex I, Chapter VI, point 2.2 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and; that individual vehicle deck surface areas are correctly measured and are also made identifiable in the vehicle approval certificates as laid down in Annex III Chapter IV of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and as required in Article (18) 1(b) of the same Regulatio

citations.text: Vehicle approval renewals are subject to the same process as new vehicles. There is extensive written guidance available for consultation for district official veterinarians (OVs) who approve vehicles for long journeys. This includes specific guidance on suitability of drinkers but not on measuring vehicle space allowances. There is no systematic training for OVs, but some have taken part in Better Training for Safer Food courses and meetings between counties and districts allow dissemination of this information. A note from NÉBIH also draws attention to the need for accurate vehicle deck areas to calculate appropriate stocking densities and to verify the suitability of drinking devices for the species of animals being transported.

The audit team reviewed vehicle approval certificates. All but one of them were inaccurate with regard to the calculation of deck surface area: many listed only an overall area for multi-deck vehicles, or the same deck surface areas for multi-deck trucks, including those with goose-neck decks at the front. This is not in compliance with the requirements necessary to correctly issue the vehicle certificate in Article 18 of Regulation 1/2005 and the specifications required to be completed in the certificate listed in Annex III Chapter IV of Regulation 1/2005. District officials relied upon the figures provided by vehicle manufacturers' which were not always accurate.

Vehicle drinking devices were not physically verified at the time of approval by the district OVs. They assumed vehicle manufacturers' would fit suitable drinkers for the species that the vehicles was listed as being capable of transporting. This is not in compliance with Article 18 of Regulation 1/2005 or in line with NÉBIH guidance. Vehicles approval certificates were issued for different species and ages of animals which would require different non-compatible drinking systems e.g. horses, rabbits, 5 calves and pigs on one certificate and would lead to some animals being unable to drink during rest stops due to the unsuitability of drinkers.

The poor standard for approval leads to a risk of inadequate space allowances and unsuitable drinking devices, during long journeys and thus to welfare problems for the animals transported. The inadequate measuring of deck floor surface areas and assessment of drinking devices at the time of approving the vehicle leads to incorrect calculations on stocking densities ­ as they are based on the deck surface area indicated in the vehicle approval certificate. Therefore, reductions in stocking density indicated in most journey logs for summer consignments are often inaccurate.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should make suitable instructions and guidance (including, if necessary diagrams) available to ensure that the requirements for suitable ventilation above transported animals, as laid down in NÉBIH existing instructions, and as required by Annex I, Chapter I, point 1,1.2 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 are implemented by transporters and correctly verified by district officials at the time of loadi

citations.text: Officials at district level did not recognise the physical limitations imposed by vehicle design height restrictions and the carriage of two decks of average height large adult cattle. There was a recent instruction issued (see also paragraph 3c above) but no clear practical guidance (vehicle and animal schematics) from NÉBIH on this. Adequate headspace and therefore ventilation was not ensured when large adult cattle (over 500kg) were transported e.g. the guidance from NÉBIH for 20cm space requirement above the withers of large bulls on two decks (which must be stacked in some way) on conventional trucks would require a minimum2 vehicle height of over 4.8m. i.e. it is not possible to load large adult cattle on two decks in conventional livestock vehicles while providing adequate headspace. This is not in compliance with Annex I, Chapter II, point 1 (1.2) of Regulation 1/2005 and NÉBIH guidance. For the most-modern, modified two- deck vehicles, and for other smaller categories of cattle this was satisfactory.

The requirements for adequate headspace and therefore ventilation provision for large adult cattle in two-tier vehicles is not respected causing unnecessary suffering to these animals during long distance transport by road to non-EU countries. The actions 7 proposed in response to previous DG SANTE recommendations on these issues were not effective as they have not been properly implemented at district level.

citations.text: Competent authorities confirmed that the national database for animals does not contain a record of geographic co-ordinates for registered pig holdings as required by Article 1 (1) (d) to Commission Decision 2000/678/EC.

The reserved rendering capacity should allow Hungary to cope with depopulation in an outbreak situation. However, in the event of confirmation of ASF, due to limitations of the database performing a census of pigs will be more time consuming and demand increased resources to localise holdings in restricted areas. In addition, there is no verification of the availability of adequate county contingency plans by the CCA. This may delay containment of disease in an outbreak scenario.

recommendations.text: To ensure that officials preforming official controls are appropriately trained, in particular as regards official sampling and assessment of labelling, as required by Article 6(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: There is a regular feed training programme whereby the representatives of the NFCSO organise training for the county and district feed safety officers on different topics. In the last three years training was provided on traceability, evaluation of laboratory results, implementation of official inspections, assessment of labelling, and implementation of official sampling. In the period 2015-2018, the central competent authority organised seven training courses per year for county and district officials in different regions. The audit team interviewed officials who had participated in these training courses but their knowledge on certain topics (e.g. labelling and official sampling) was not sufficient (see findings 35 and 45).

Despite the fact that training had been provided on the legal requirements of feed labelling (see finding 4), county feed inspectors were generally unable to apply this knowledge during official inspections, and thus to undertake their duties competently, (see finding 33 and 34) which is not line with requirements of Article 6(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections

Regular and thorough verification of the FeBOs' own control and traceability systems strengthens the effectiveness of the official controls. However, significant weaknesses were seen on the verification of labelling requirements during official controls. The training provided does not support the official control staff to undertake their duties competently. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

The audit team noted that, in spite of the centrally-developed guidance document on the practical aspects of official sampling (see finding 42) and training provided (see finding 4) on the legal requirements of official sampling, county feed safety inspectors, as opposed to the performance of official sampling carried out by the Food and Feed Safety Directorate of the NFCSO, were not aware of the guidance document with the result of them failing to follow the requirements on official sampling laid down by Commission Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. This calls into question the appropriateness of the training provided under the requirements of Article 6(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The system in place for planning of official sampling is risk-based. However, the legal and analytical validity of official sampling is weakened by systematic deficiencies on the implementation of official sampling by county feed safety inspectors thus, severely undermining the effectiveness of the official sampling system. The training provided does not support county officials to undertake their duties competently. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

recommendations.text: To ensure that feed business operators meet the labelling requirements as required by Article 16 of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003 and Article 15 of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009.

citations.text: Whilst verification of labelling had been regularly carried out during previous county inspections, no non-compliances had been identified during such official controls. Despite this, the audit team was able to identify numerous and significant shortcomings on labelling at the majority of establishments visited. Examples of shortcomings were: 7 The identification number of several feed additives not being present on the label, which is a legal requirement of Article 16(1)(f) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003. Identification of feed materials used as a carrier for feed additives production was not included on the labelling as required by Article 16(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. Feed material being labelled as feed additive, which is not in line with the requirements of Article 15(a) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009. Labels were seen for various premixtures from different producers stating that "the premix contains additional vitamins and micro-elements (beyond those listed) based on the agreement with the buyer and defined in the technical specifications (with no such detailed technical specification available) ". This is not in line with the requirements of Article 16(1)(a)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 1831/2003.

Furthermore, in some cases county inspectors could not explain how to assess the laboratory results of official samples related to control of declared concentrations (e.g. coccidiostats in a premixture for broilers, vitamin A in a pre-mixture for fattening pigs).

Regular and thorough verification of the FeBOs' own control and traceability systems strengthens the effectiveness of the official controls. However, significant weaknesses were seen on the verification of labelling requirements during official controls. The training provided does not support the official control staff to undertake their duties competently. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

To take appropriate action to verify that the operational arrangements made by the county CA to apply the national contingency plan for avian influenza, in particular in relation to availability of adequately trained staff and equipment; are fit for purpose so that an effective early response, particularly in the event of a widespread disease outbreak affecting an area with a high density of poultry, can be deployed without delay. citations.text: BACKGROUND Controls on residues and contaminants and the use of veterinary medicinal products in Hungary were previously audited by the Commission in 2012 (2) and the 2012 report concluded that the system of residue monitoring was in compliance with EU legislation. However, the overall effectiveness of the residue monitoring plan was compromised by weaknesses in laboratory performance and, in particular, by deficiencies in implementation and a lack of effective supervision thereof. All five audit report recommendations were satisfactorily addressed.

recommendations.text: To ensure that (a) the required numbers of samples are taken as planned for all commodities, as required by Annex IV to Directive 96/23/EC, (b) that sampling strategy satisfies the requirements to avoid multiple sampling from the same producer (as required by point 2.3.3.1. of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC) and (c) that sampling strategy allows trace back to the producer in the event of a non- compliant result being detected (Point A of Chapter 4 of the Annex to Commission Decision 97/747/EC).

citations.text: The 2018 national residue monitoring plan was largely implemented as foreseen with the exception of eggs and caprine/ovine milk. For eggs 75% of planned samples were taken and for ovine milk 80% (60% in 2019). For caprine milk 70% and 20% of planned samples were taken in 2018 and 2019 respectively, which is not in line with EU law (17).

There is currently no mechanism in place to identify and thus allow either the counties or the central competent authority to prevent multiple sampling from the same operator, as required by EU law (19). The Hadju Bihar county staff stated that under the current system they do not receive copies of the sampling reports sent by the district veterinarians to the testing laboratories. Therefore they cannot verify if multiple sampling from the same operator takes place. Similarly staff from the NFCSO confirmed that they did not supervise and verify if this requirement had been respected by the counties. Thus the actions foreseen to address recommendation No 2 of the 2012 audit report with regards to ensuring that no multiple sampling from the same operator takes place, were not effective.

However, the audit team received a copy of a letter sent during the time of the audit from the Secretary of State to all counties asking staff to pay attention to the fact that samples should not be taken from the same establishments and rather to sample as many establishments and animal holdings as possible. The competent authority further expressed its intention to create a supervision mechanism to avoid multiple sampling from the same operator.

Both the national and Baranya county sampling data indicate that samples from honey were frequently taken at retail level. Sampling blended honey decreases the chances of identifying non-compliant results (due to dilution) and, even if non- compliant results were identified, tracing back to the offending producer, as required by EU legislation (20), would be difficult.

The absence of supervision of implementation has contributed to weaknesses such as multiple sampling of the same producer, under-sampling of certain commodities and sampling strategies (in the case of honey) which militate against detection of residues and compromise traceability in the event of non-compliant results being detected. 5.1.4. citations.text: The audit team evaluated the follow-up investigations for the six cases, all of which concerned antimicrobials in pigs, poultry and cattle. - in one case (oxytetracycline and doxycycline in porcine tissue) the applicable follow-up procedures were followed, the cause of the non-compliance was identified and a deterrent fine imposed in line with EU legislation (24). - In five of the six cases, evidence was provided that affected product was traced and if still present, destroyed to safeguard public health, which is in line with EU law (27). - In three cases, written records of the follow-up investigation did not include a description of the control methods applied at farm level or the outcome of such official control. Articles 3 of Decision (EU) 2018/1136 Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 26 and

citations.text: The competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team to confirm that the NFCSO had carried out any recent assessment to identify specific risk factors regarding the introduction in, and the transmission within and between poultry holdings of HPAI. Representatives of the NFCSO indicated that they consider the entire country to be a high-risk area. However, the epidemiological evidence from the previous epizootic, indicates that there are risk factors associated with specific geographical locations that experienced HPAI outbreaks in Hungary in the past. Those factors include the areas with a high density of domestic waterfowl. Although the audit team found evidence that the competent authorities did not have up-to-date information in relation to the number, location, size and density of all commercial and non-commercial holdings in those areas (see finding 36), the high density of birds in those areas is a well-known reality. In addition, poultry in those areas are often in open-air holdings and the frequency of movements between holdings is very high. These are areas through which migratory birds travel or have some of their resting areas. This is not in line with requirements laid down in Article 3(1) of Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1136, which requires that Member States identify the areas of their territory that are at particular risk for the introduction of HPAI viruses into poultry holdings.

The NFCSO did not update the risk profile of those areas taking into account the epidemiological evidence of an increasing threat posed by the detection of HPAI. They did 7 not update the profile after confirmation of the first outbreaks in Hungary in January, and despite the presence of HPAI infection in migratory wild birds in neighbouring Member States. This is not in line with requirements laid down in Article 3(3) of Decision (EU) 2018/1136. Nevertheless, the competent authorities took some actions to reinforce the application of generic risk mitigation and biosecurity measures in the whole country (see the next points).

citations.text: After confirmation of the first outbreaks in January 2020, the NFCSO issued CVO Decision 1/2020, ordering the enclosed housing of poultry in the territory of the whole country. This is in line with requirements on risk mitigation of HPAI laid down in Article 4.4(b) of Decision (EU) 2018/1136. CVO Decision 03/2017 had already established that keepers of commercial poultry holdings throughout the country should apply certain biosecurity requirements, and that the county and district veterinary services should regularly check and enforce them. CVO Decision 03/2017 also establishes specific requirements on stocking levels of poultry. It provides that stocking of poultry cannot be authorised if the holdings do not meet the other biosecurity requirements. However, the competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team to confirm that the competent authorities had carried out official controls to ensure the implementation and enforce the risk mitigation and biosecurity measures laid down in those Decisions, in particular in the potential high-risk areas mentioned previously. This is not in line with requirements of Article 10(1) of Decision (EU) 2018/1136.

The competent authorities assessed the official controls carried out in 2018 to verify compliance with CVO Decision 03/2017. They concluded that there had been some improvements in the implementation of biosecurity standards, when compared with 2016/17. They have not carried out similar assessments since 2018, and the competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team to confirm that they had enforced CVO Decision 3/2017 during the first months of 2020. This is not in line with Article 10(1) of Decision (EU) 2018/1136.

The competent authorities decided that the absence of wild bird cases was a reason for not implementing further mitigating measures in high-risk areas after the first outbreaks detected in January 2020. Despite the temporary exception mentioned above for Bács-Kiskun County, The competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team to confirm implementation of the increased surveillance of wild bird populations or the further monitoring for dead or sick wild birds since the first cases of HPAI were detected in January. This is not in line with Article 4(1)(b) of Directive 2005/94/EC, which requires Member States to carry out surveillance in wild birds to contribute, on the basis of a regularly updated risk assessment, to the knowledge of the threats posed by wild birds. This is not in line either with Article 8 of Decision (EU) 2018/1136, which requires Member States to carry out increased surveillance in wild bird populations.

citations.text: Regardless of which form the competent authorities used, the investigation forms that the audit team examined rarely reached conclusions on the likely length of time during which avian influenza may have been present on the holding or on the possible sources of the infection, as required by Article 6(2) of Directive 2005/94/EC. The approach taken to carry out the epidemiological investigations was not standardised or consistent along the epizootic, and there was a persistent lack of quality and completeness of the data obtained. This, in many cases, did not allow the competent authorities to investigate all the elements contained in points (a) to (d) of Article 6(2) of Directive 2005/94/EC.

The shortcomings described in the previous points precluded the NDCC from taking fully into account the results of the epidemiological inquiries to take well-informed decisions to: a) apply and adapt additional disease control measures, as necessary for each outbreak or affected area, and b) grant derogations to the restrictions applied as a result of the outbreaks. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 6(3) of Directive 2005/94/EC. 5.1.1.3 Handling of confirmation ­ Derogations

The audit team confirmed that when they established the protection and surveillance zones in response to confirmed HPAI outbreaks, the LDCCs did not carry out the poultry censuses of all holdings in the protection zone, as required by Article 18 of Directive 2005/94/EC, and of all commercial poultry holdings in the surveillance zones, as required by Article 30 of Directive 2005/94/EC. The NDCC and the LDCCs relied exclusively on the national holding registration system (TIR system) to identify the holdings, to monitor and inform them about 14 the restrictions in those zones. The TIR system is not updated regularly, which prevents the competent authorities from having a properly updated contingency plan giving an indication of the number, location, size and density of commercial holdings, as required by Article 62(2) of, and points 10 and 12 of Annex X to Directive 2005/94/EC. It does not include either information on non-commercial farms. The competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team the total number of non-commercial farms in the protection or surveillance zones. This is not in line with Article 16(3)(c) of Directive 2005/94/EC. They also could not provide information requested by the audit team to demonstrate whether all farms, in particular those in the protection zones, were included in the screening and surveillance activities required by EU legislation for the control of the infection. This is not in line with requirements in that respect laid down in Articles 18(b) and 29(1) of Directive 2005/94/EC. 5.1.3.2 Further restricted zones

To address recommendation 7 made in the report of the previous audit, the revised national contingency plan requires the competent authorities to plan depopulation activities in line with the requirements of Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009, in order to avoid potential animal welfare problems. A specific form is included in the contingency plan for this purpose. However, the competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team that the local competent authorities prepared depopulation plans and, consequently, that they had carried out that activity in accordance with those plans. Instead, they relied on their experience from previous epizootics and their knowledge of the requirements. This is not in compliance with paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Article mentioned above. 18

The routine method of killing used was sublimed dry ice (the solid form of carbon dioxide, which usually sublimes at around ­78.5ºC) within closed containers. The local veterinarians did not report any difficulties killing waterfowl using this method, but one of the more experienced veterinarians highlighted the difficulty of preventing contact between the birds and the sublimed dry ice. The officials did not fully monitor the temperature and carbon dioxide concentrations to render safely the birds insensible. Therefore, despite the guarantees provided by the competent authorities to address recommendation 7 of the previous audit, they have not applied the measures undertaken to do that in a satisfactory manner. This does not comply with Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 as it is not one of the methods listed for killing domestic waterfowl in Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009. Moreover, the use of that killing method is not in line with requirements laid down in Chapter II of that Annex (point 8) and Article 18(2) of the said Regulation. 5.1.4.2 Disposal of carcases

During the epizootic, there were also important delays on the depopulation of other outbreaks (see also finding 21), taking up to more than 14 days in some cases (e.g. ADNS reference 2020-251). Therefore, despite the guarantees provided by the competent authorities to address recommendation 8 of the previous audit report, they have not applied the measures undertaken to do that in a satisfactory manner. This does not comply with Article 11(2) of Directive 2005/94/EC, as downstream delays in disposal of carcases resulted in upstream delays in slaughtering poultry on holdings where outbreaks were confirmed. It is not in line either with requirements of Annex X (point 5) to the said Directive, as the competent authorities did not ensure that the necessary equipment and materials were available for the disposal of carcasses, a fundamental measure for the effective control of HPAI. The NFCSO updated the national contingency plan following the recommendation 1 of the previous audit. However, the competent authorities did not implement some of these updates (e.g., categorisation of areas at risk, use of guidance for depopulation, quick carcass disposal and census of holdings in restricted areas). This is not in line with Article 5(1)(i) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which requires that Member States be prepared to operate their contingency plans in the event of an emergency.

Each county is obliged to develop and keep updated its own contingency plan, based on the national model, but including information and guidance tailored to the specific needs of the county. The audit team checked as an example the contingency plan in Bács-Kiskun County and found that it does not include important information for the rapid control of the epizootic 21 in that county and that it had not been updated since the last epizootic. The missing information includes, for instance, a list of stakeholders' contacts, indication of the availability of equipment and materials necessary for the effective control of the disease, and information on the skills and responsibilities of staff. This does not comply with the requirements laid down in Article 62(1) and (2) of, and Annex X (paragraphs 3, 4 and 5) to Directive 2005/94/EC. The central competent authorities have not verified and corrected appropriately the contingency plans of the counties affected by the 2020 HPAI epizootic. Taking into account that national arrangements on contingency planning require that the national plan is completed and updated with its adaptation to each county's specific conditions, that incompleteness and lack of verification is not in compliance with Articles 5(1)(i) and 12(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.2.2 Registration of poultry holdings ­ Areas with high density of poultry

Despite CVO Decision 03/2017 establishing the requirement to inform and obtain official approval for the introduction of poultry, the TIR system is not fully up to date and does not have records of non-commercial holdings. The TIR system includes many holdings that are not active (3,000 holdings are registered, of which approximately 50% keep birds at a point in time). As explained in previous sections, that shortcoming has compromised the quality of the epidemiological investigations, caused delays in identifying all holdings within the restricted zones and contact and at-risk holdings, and precluded that the competent authorities could analyse the epidemiological situation in order to consider whether there was a need to avail of the additional measures provided by Articles 10(1) and (2), and 15(2) of Directive 2005/94/EC. This, together with the absence of a comprehensive on-site census in protection and surveillance zones during the epizootic (see finding 36), is not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 6(2), 16(3)(c) and 62(2) of, and with Annex X (points 10 and 12) to Directive 2005/94/EC.

Despite the information included in point 76 above, the situations described in the previous points were caused by the limited availability of suitably qualified and experienced staff ­ many of them natural persons who had been delegated some official control tasks and other official activities ­ who had not received appropriate training to perform their duties competently in the context of this animal health emergency. This is not in compliance with requirements laid down in Articles 5(1)(e) and (4), 30(b)(i) and (ii) and 31(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and in Annex X (point 7) to Directive 2005/94/EC. citations.text: In March 2020, the NDCC ordered the prompt depopulation of all poultry present on the first affected holdings and on the holdings within the protection zones established in Bács-Kiskun and Csongrád Counties. Taking into account the fast evolution of the disease and the high 11 density of poultry present in the area, after those first cases, the competent authorities decided in accordance with Article 10(1) and (3) of Directive 2005/94/EC, to apply the measures provided for in Article 11 to holdings where outbreaks were suspected. However, the limited transport and carcase disposal capacity caused important delays in many of those cases. As a result, 78% of the outbreaks detected after March were depopulated three or more days after suspicion was reported; 49% at four or more days and 33% at five or more days and up to more than two weeks (e.g. ADNS reference 2020-121). Therefore, the competent authorities did not apply the intended measures in line with Article 11(1) to (3) of Directive 2005/94/EC. Those limitations delayed as well the application of preventive slaughtering and killing of poultry from contact holdings and from non-affected holdings within the protection zones in accordance with the options provided by Articles 15(2) and 17(3) of the said Directive.

The previous audit reported delays in the disposal of carcases due to limited rendering capacity. The competent authorities addressed this problem in their action plan, ensuring an increase in rendering capacity for a maximum of six weeks in case of an emergency. On 28 May, in the communication to the Commission mentioned in section 5.1.3.3 (point 43), they indicated that the required rendering capacity had been available throughout the epizootic and that the rendering plants were working in longer shifts and during weekends. However, during this audit, they confirmed that, due to initial low rendering capacity, there were delays in depopulation of outbreaks and of preventive culling in the protection zone set on 26 March. The competent authorities used burial sites only for a few carcases because of technical difficulties with site selection.

During the epizootic, there were also important delays on the depopulation of other outbreaks (see also finding 21), taking up to more than 14 days in some cases (e.g. ADNS reference 2020-251). Therefore, despite the guarantees provided by the competent authorities to address recommendation 8 of the previous audit report, they have not applied the measures undertaken to do that in a satisfactory manner. This does not comply with Article 11(2) of Directive 2005/94/EC, as downstream delays in disposal of carcases resulted in upstream delays in slaughtering poultry on holdings where outbreaks were confirmed. It is not in line either with requirements of Annex X (point 5) to the said Directive, as the competent authorities did not ensure that the necessary equipment and materials were available for the disposal of carcasses, a fundamental measure for the effective control of HPAI. citations.text: In response to recommendation 6 from the previous audit, the NFCSO introduced new arrangements to assess the epidemiological risks before granting derogations from the measures applicable in restricted zones as required by Article 33(1) of Directive 2005/94/EC. That includes using a risk assessment form, which forms part of the revised national contingency plan (Annex VII-paragraph 18a). Most of the assessments reviewed by the audit team did not cover all relevant risks and it was not clear whether they took account of the local epidemiological situation and were sufficiently informative for the competent authorities to ensure, before granting the derogations, that they would not endanger HPAI 15 control (see next points for examples in that respect). This is not fully in line with Article 33(5) of Directive 2005/94/EC, which provides that derogations shall only be granted if they do not endanger disease control.

The audit team confirmed that most of the criteria laid down in Annex IV to Directive 2005/94/EC, some of which the competent authorities had taken into account to decide on the application of preventive culling in accordance with Articles 15(2) and 17(3) of the said Directive, were applicable to the relevant restricted zones. Therefore, increasing the density of poultry in those high-risk zones ­ a derogation that should have been based on a risk assessment carried out in accordance with Article 33(1) of the said Directive ­ while applying those measures conducive to reduce quickly the density of susceptible poultry, was a contradiction that may have undermined the objective pursued with the application of the former two articles.

The competent authorities detected 24 outbreaks during pre-movement testing: 23 of them in movements granted for direct slaughter and one to force-feeding. The competent authority could not provide the evidence requested by the audit team on the risk assessments required by Article 33 of Directive 2005/94/EC that the competent authorities should have undertaken prior to these movements being authorised or on possible epidemiological links to previous outbreaks.

The impressive amount of PCR tests carried out during the epizootic, in excess of 30,000 (approximately 70% between 25 March and 8 June), used for testing some 130,000 swabs from live poultry and tissues from poultry carcasses, cast doubts on the alleged limited analytical capacity of the NRL in that respect. As indicated in the report of the previous audit, the numerous derogations granted to holdings in the restricted zones overstretch significantly the testing capacity of the NRL (i.e. in 2020, derogations required PCR testing of tens of thousands of samples). This is not in line with Annex X (point 8) to Directive 2005/94/EC. 25

audits.title: Official controls on animal by-products (ABP) and derived products (DP)

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when granting approval for ABP processing plants, the operator meets all of the infrastructure and equipment requirements for a plant and, in particular, has put in place appropriate own checks and HACCP-based procedures, including validation of the processing plant.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 44 of Regulation (EC) 1069/2009, Section 2 of Chapter I in Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011;

citations.text: In the regions visited, the audit team interviewed the county officials responsible for granting approvals, examined a number of approval files and documents presented by operators of ABP plants visited and noted numerous and repetitive inconsistencies related to the approval process. Thus, approvals had been granted without: a. proper assessment of the reliability of the operators' own checks, b. official controls on operators' validation (including on processing method 7), c. proper assessment of operators' HACCP-based procedures, and d. an on-site visit, to verify if the plant complied with all of the legal requirements, and in particular, those related to (i) the prevention of cross-contamination between ABP of different categories and (ii) the equipment required for the processing method notified for approval. The above findings are not in line with requirements of Articles 44 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, and Section 2 of Annex XVI and Letter G in Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The CGO and NFCSO representatives met explained that these inconsistencies in the approval process resulted from misinterpretation of the applicable approval requirements by the officials concerned.

Whilst the legal basis for the registration, approval and listing of ABP plants is in line with EU requirements, implementation of the approval process was deficient resulting in unwarranted approvals being granted by the NFCSO and operators who did not meet all of the legal requirements, commencing their operations, thus undermining confidence in the proper functioning of the ABP chain. 5.2.2 Planning of official controls

In audited regions, the audit team reassessed documents held by operators, observed the operators' on-site activities, compared these with records from the most recent official controls (including for the purpose of the approval/re-approval process), and noted that official controls either overlooked and/or misinterpreted a number of requirements. For example, there was a lack of proper: a. Verification of the information entered by operators in the documents accompanying the ABP consignments (commercial documents) which otherwise would have allowed the officials to identify that additional activities were taking place for which operators did not have the required approval/authorisation; b. Assessment of operators' HACCP-based procedures related to processing methods used, in particular, to the processing parameters and their critical limits; 10 c. Checks on the processing plants' validation demonstrating the effectiveness of processing method 7; d. Assessment of the reliability of the operators' own checks related to sampling, in particular, on microbiological standards (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae and E.coli) and on the content of glyceroltriheptanoate used for marking of DP of the Category 1 and 2 material; e. Official sampling (see finding 28c) and the performance checks related to glyceroltriheptanoate. 5.2.3.3 Actions taken in the event of non-compliance and follow-up

recommendations.text: To ensure that all types of operators acting along the entire chain of ABP and DP are subject to official controls.

citations.text: The audit team analysed documents related to the planning of official controls and noted that in 2020 and 2021, the NFSCO did not use the above-stated algorithm for planning controls but rather adjusted its inspection programmes manually. Consequently, in these years the NFCSO selected operators, establishments and plants with the following four activities: 1) operators handling animal by-products inside the European Union and in third countries: (https://ec.europa.eu/food/system/files/2021-09/animal-products_approved-establishments_abp_tech- specs.pdf) 7 transport of ABP, 2) collection of ABP, 3) processing of ABP, and 4) using ABP for special feeding purposes.

The NFSCO representatives explained that in 2019, the rules of domestic legislation resulted in/triggered complete migration of data on the ABP operators to the electronic IT-based risk assessment system. Prior to the migration, information on some operators was available only in a paper form at the county and district levels. Thus, the list of ABP operators in the IT- based risk assessment system for planning official controls was inaccurate ­ lacking a significant number of operators. Therefore, the manual adjustment was necessary to establish if all registered and/or approved ABP/DP operators, establishments and plants remained active at the time of the migration. Due to the high number of operators covered, the NFCSO extended its controls from 2020 to 2021 stressing that the manual selection was temporary and that district inspectors could carry out additional controls also on other types of operators aside from those planned, for example when ordered to do so by the NFCSO or where there was a public complaint or a case of suspicion.

With respect to the above, the audit team noted that: a. In none of the regions visited had the district inspectors met carried out any additional controls or focussed their inspections on the ABP plants/operators representing the above-mentioned four types of activities. b. In one region visited, there were numerous incinerators and, at least from 2017, the district inspectors had not carried out an ABP inspection on any of them. The above is not in line with requirements of Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The CGO and the DGO representatives met explained that the overall number of controls planned in all areas for which the district officials are responsible is so high that, with the current resources, the district inspectors do not plan any additional controls. Conclusion on planning of official controls

As designed, the system for planning official controls, in principle, takes into account the relevant risk criteria. However, this is undermined by the fact that the information on at least two of the planning criteria is unreliable (the result of the last inspections and reliability of operators' own checks). Furthermore, the fact that several types of operators have been excluded from the planning process, weakens assurances that the entire ABP/DP chain is adequately controlled. 5.2.3 Implementation of official controls

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls accurately assess operators' documentation and the results of operators' own checks and that the resulting reports provide a reliable picture of the activities of those establishments generating, collecting, handling and processing ABP, so that the risk-based planning of official controls is improved.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 9(1) of Regulation 2017/625, Section 1 of Chapter I in Annex XVI to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011;

citations.text: The NFCSO has in place training arrangements for its staff covering general aspects of administrative and official controls rules and a sector-specific development. Trainings vary in form and range from those with personal participation (mostly pre-COVID pandemic) to on- line courses (during the COVID pandemic). The audit team examined evidence of training, interviewed ABP inspectors met and noted that: a. The CGOs' and DGOs do not specialise in selected types controls but multitask, covering many different controls, e.g. on animal health and welfare, food and feed hygiene, ABP, etc. 4 b. Prior to the COVID-pandemic, the authority regularly organised on-site, training courses inviting the staff from the county and district offices. During the COVID- pandemic, trainings were delivered by e-learning. The training courses usually covered various control-related topics, including some aspects related specifically to ABP. c. Officials' awareness of ABP requirements was inconsistent, with many misinterpretations of requirements and/or overlooking of various requirements applicable both to official controls and to ABP operators, establishments and plants and, in particular, the approval process for operators, the assessment of operators' HACCP-based procedures and the assessment of operators' own checks and ABP- related sampling requirements (see Section 5.2). The above training arrangement, in principle, complies with requirement of Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, except for point (a) of the said Article.

The constituent parts of the official control system are in place, vis-á-vis legal framework, designation of competent authorities, provision of adequate and appropriate laboratory capacity and an internal audit system capable of identifying problems in the implementation of official controls in this sector. Nevertheless and in spite of the training programme provided for control staff, fundamental misinterpretations of various ABP requirements as evidenced by interview of control staff and examination of official control records in parallel with operators' documentation (see conclusion 35), indicate that this key requirement of the control system is not functioning effectively. Whilst official controls are performed on the ABP chain, their effectiveness and appropriateness is substantially undermined by a fundamental misinterpretation of the requirements applicable to operators as evidenced by the numerous deficiencies and discrepancies between the content of the official control records and the operators' records, observed by the audit team. Whilst the absence of monitoring/supervision in relation to ABP controls is also an issue, overall, the controls, as currently applied are not fit for their intended purpose and provide little in the way of assurances that the ABP/DP production and distribution chain in Hungary functions in line with EU requirements.

audits.title: Imports of animals and goods and verification of compliance of border control posts with Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that documented procedures for the conduct of official controls on food of non-animal origin are updated as appropriate.

citations.text: The NFCSO-DPPSCA has issued two specific documented procedures for the official controls on imports of consignments of food of non-animal origin for the presence of aflatoxins and unauthorised genetically modified organisms in rice products originating in China. No documented procedures or instructions for performing official controls on imports of other food of non-animal origin had been issued at the time of the audit, which is not in line with Article 12(1) of the OCR.

The NFCSO-DPPSCA informed the audit team that it was in the process of updating its Authority's Guide, which is aimed at controls on food of non-animal origin in the Single Market, to include guidance on performing official controls on imports of such products listed in Annexes I and II.1 to Regulation (EU) 2019/1793. The NFCSO-DPPSCA stated that the update was due to be completed by January 2022.

However, the lack of documented procedures for the performance of official controls on food of non-animal origin, has the potential to undermine assurances that such controls are sufficient to minimise, as far as possible, the introduction of non-compliant consignments into the Union. 11 5.2 IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON IMPORTS/TRANSITS OF ANIMALS AND GOODS

audits.title: Follow up audit - evaluate the implementation of actions regarding recommendations of audit DG(SANTE)2020-6989

recommendations.text: To ensure that all analytical methods used for the residue monitoring are fit for intended use and are properly validated.

citations.text: Initial validation data for screening of stilbenes and steroids were revised by the laboratory in response to the findings made in the 2020 audit report (see finding 32 of that report) to eliminate most of the obvious discrepancies. However, some data at the lowest calibration levels still showed that the performance characteristics (e.g., identical repeatability and reproducibility values for methylboldenone and 17- clostebol chlorandrostenedione) were not in line with legal requirements (8). These shortcomings in the method performance characteristics were neither spotted nor evaluated by the laboratory. In addition, the calculation of CC was not in line with legal provisions (9).

In the method validation file for confirmation of thyrostats, a number of recoveries were outside the acceptable range laid down in EU legislation (10). This was not noticed by the laboratory and thus no assessment of the possible influence of that phenomenon on the suitability of the method had been carried out. The linearity of the calibration curve for propylthiouracil was below the criteria set by the laboratory ­ however, this was not reflected and concluded on in the validation documentation. The laboratory representative informed the audit team that the revalidation of the method was planned for 2025.

In the validation documentation for the screening and confirmatory method for beta- agonists, there was inadequate assessment of several method performance characteristics (e.g., recoveries outside the established range (10), reproducibilities identical to repeatabilities (8)).

At the time of the audit, the screening and confirmatory method for chloramphenicol, thiamphenicol and florfenicol was under validation. Consequently, no properly validated method was available in the laboratory for monitoring residues of these analytes.

The validation of the screening method for antibacterial substances was stated to be finalised just prior to the audit. The available documentation included only data on specificity and results of measurements at one fortification level for each analyte/matrix combination. This level was assumed as the CC with no justification for that decision. This is not in line with legal requirements (11). Since the validation did not address all of the performance characteristics required for quantitative screening methods (12), the method could not be considered as properly validated.

The validation report for the coccidiostats confirmatory method dated from 2014 and contained implausibly identical values for repeatabilities and reproducibilities (8) and numerous recoveries outside the established range (10). These observations were not commented on in the validation documentation. Moreover, during the routine application of the method, the analyst met stated that "no CC were used due to erroneous values obtained during the validation". Thus, at the time of the audit, there (8) Part 2.3.2.2. of Annex I to Decision 2002/657/EC and part 1.2.2.2. of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2021/808.
