(10) Part 2.3.2.1. of Annex I to Decision 2002/657/EC and part 1.2.2.1. of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2021/808. (11) Part 2.7.(2) of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2021/808. (12) Part 2.1. of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2021/808. 4 was no properly validated method in this laboratory for coccidiostats. The laboratory representative informed the audit team that a new validation was planned for 2022.

Validation data from 2014 for confirmation of sedatives were reassessed by the laboratory in response to the 2020 audit report. However, a number of recoveries were still outside the required range established in the EU (10). Again, these shortcomings were not noted in the most recent validation documentation (e.g., for chlorpromazine and propionilpromazine). Furthermore, the fortification levels used for azaperone and carazolol were lower than the relevant maximum residue limits (MRLs) established in EU (13) and thus no correct determination of CC was possible in these circumstances (14).

The validation data from 2016 for the screening and confirmatory method for NSAIDs were reassessed by the laboratory in response to the 2020 audit report. As a result, the laboratory found the method unsuitable for a number of analytes and a new validation was planned for May 2022. However, the unsuitable method was still in use for routine testing of residue monitoring samples.

For all of the methods scrutinised, the laboratory had no practice to analyse and evaluate data obtained during the method validation experiments and consequently no conclusions on any of these methods' fitness for their intended use were made.

During the validations, analyte stability and ruggedness had not been assessed at all though required (15) and this had already been brought to the attention of the laboratory staff during the 2020 audit (see finding 29 of the 2020 audit report). Only for the beta-agonists method had the laboratory presented data on analyte stability in matrix which had been compiled by the relevant European Union Reference Laboratory (EURL). However, the conditions cited by the EURL were not identical with those in the laboratory and thus the data cannot be used solely as evidence of adequate assessment of the analyte stability (16). During the routine use of the thyrostat method, there was no consideration of instability of the analytes during freezing/thawing cycles and during storage in a freezer (17) which may affect the analytical validity of such samples. The lack of information about analyte stability, in combination with lengthy turnaround times (e.g., up to four months for antimicrobials) can undermine the analytical validity of the results (i.e. truly non- compliant samples may not be detected).

Overall, the actions taken by the laboratory to rectify method validation deficiencies identified during the 2020 audit, were neither sufficiently effective nor comprehensive enough to satisfactorily address Recommendation 5 of the 2020 audit report. (18) 5.2.2. Quality control

The actions taken to rectify deficiencies identified during the 2020 audit concerning method validation and internal quality control at the FTNRL were insufficient to satisfactorily address the relevant recommendations. Whilst outsourcing of laboratory testing is planned, the absence of appropriate designation of those facilities potentially weakens the effectiveness of this measure.

This is not in line with legal requirements (19); b. there were a number of cases where the calculation of results had been made well outside the working range of the calibration curve without any justification given in the quality control documentation (e.g., calculation of nicarbazin levels). In addition, on numerous occasions, the results for one matrix were calculated on the basis of a calibration curve based on another, not equivalent matrix (e.g., calibration curves created on the basis of chicken muscle were routinely used to calculate results for pig kidney) despite the fact that such an approach was questioned during the 2020 audit (see finding 34 in the 2020 audit report); c. acceptability ranges for the calibration curve parameters were largely well described which is in line with legal requirements (20). However, the audit team noted three occasions where the coefficient of determination (R2) was below the set criterion without any documented action in the quality control documentation (e.g., 4-aminoantipyrine and N-formyl-4-aminoantipyrine in milk); d. quality control charts were seen for all of the methods scrutinised and were based on recovery of fortified samples. Control charts were updated with up to three months delay (due to a high workload as explained by the analysts met). There was no routine assessment of quality control results. The audit team saw a number of cases where the recovery levels were outside the acceptability range without any note/action in the quality control documentation (e.g., control charts for nicarbazin and N-methyl-4-aminoantipyrine). The audit team also saw an adequate quality control procedure which included relevant criteria of the control charts' assessment, however it was not implemented for the methods scrutinised during the audit. These findings indicate that the actions taken by the laboratory with regard to the internal quality control deficiencies identified during the 2020 audit were not in line with legal requirements and Recommendation 6 of the 2020 audit report has not been satisfactorily addressed. 5.2.3. Equipment, subcontracting and laboratory designation

The actions taken to rectify deficiencies identified during the 2020 audit concerning method validation and internal quality control at the FTNRL were insufficient to satisfactorily address the relevant recommendations. Whilst outsourcing of laboratory testing is planned, the absence of appropriate designation of those facilities potentially weakens the effectiveness of this measure.

citations.text: The system in place for the control of ASF in wild boar is effective. The constant reduction in wild boar density over the last three years should help the authorities to slow down the spread of the disease. The effective passive surveillance, the good testing and correct disposal of carcases helps preventing the spread of the disease from wild animals.

The authorities use unclear risk criteria to decide how many and which establishments the counties should target for their biosecurity inspections. Their control plan is poorly implemented and the authorities do not inspect the vast majority of small commercial establishments and non-commercial ones. Therefore, for these sectors, the authorities are not aware of level of compliance with basic 8 requirements, the degree of preparation to avoid the entry and spread of ASF and the awareness of operators regarding the disease. This is a major risk to prevent the disease entering such establishments and to detect the disease promptly if this happened.

The competent authority maintains that there are no "outdoor" pig establishments in Hungary as defined in the EU strategy for ASF, although they keep a list of "outdoor" pig establishments and there are establishments allowing pig access to outdoor pens. The absence of legal definition of "outdoor establishments" creates different interpretations between officials2. All this creates some uncertainty when evaluating the risk of introduction of ASF.

The contingency plans at county level are still incomplete, as they lack guidance for depopulation, information regarding availability of equipment and materials necessary for the effective control of the disease and provisions to dispose of the carcases safely and quickly. This compromises the readiness of Hungary to deal effectively with outbreaks in the event that ASF is confirmed in domestic pigs.

audits.title: evaluate the application of measures for the control of highly pathogenic avian influenza

recommendations.text: To ensure that all poultry establishments that pose a significant risk to the epidemiology of avian influenza in the country are registered and their associated information is updated and, for establishments excluded from registration requirements, have evidence that they do not have an active role in the HPAI epidemics. Articles 84, 85, 93, 101 (1)(a) and 108(4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1345 and Article 18 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2035. , and

citations.text: Background The 2021­2022 HPAI epidemic season was the largest observed in Europe, with a total of 2,467 outbreaks in poultry, 47.7 million birds culled in the affected establishments, 187 outbreaks in captive birds, and 3,573 HPAI virus detections in wild birds to an unprecedented geographical extent reaching from Svalbard islands to South Portugal and Ukraine, affecting 37 European countries (EFSA overview, 2023). An unprecedented number of HPAI virus detections were reported in wild and domestic birds in Europe from June to September 2022. The persistence of the virus in wild birds indicated that it may have become endemic in the wild bird populations in Europe. Up to May 2023, the number of HPAI outbreaks in poultry during the season 2022-2023 has decreased in Europe in comparison with the previous year (2021-2022). Since November 2021 until beginning of the audit Hungary notified 73 outbreaks in wild birds and 464 outbreaks in poultry. In 2021, the authorities reported 98 outbreaks in domestic poultry (six in backyards and the rest in commercial establishments). In 2022 the number of reported outbreaks in poultry went up to 280, seven in backyard poultry and the rest in commercial establishments (vast majority in waterfowl). In 2023, the country reported additional 79 outbreaks in poultry (up to 28 July), again majority (67) in waterfowl (mainly foie-gras production) (for more see Table 1 in Annex 2). Geographically, the outbreaks in this period were mostly clustered in the South of Hungary. Furthermore, from November 2021 to February 2022, the authorities detected four outbreaks in captive birds and two additional ones in January/March 2023. 2 4. Main findings and conclusions Registration 1. The authorities register poultry establishments including their location and size in the national holding registration system (TIR). The system also provides information on the type of establishment, species kept, start and any cessation of its operation. 2. According to the national legislation all flocks with 2,000 broilers or more and those with 500 adult birds or more must be registered. In addition, the registration is required for all commercial establishments, notwithstanding the number of birds they keep. 3. The authorities exempted from the registration requirement non-commercial (backyard) poultry establishments as they consider them compliant with criteria laid down in Article 3 of Regulation 2022/1345. The authority also considers the risk of those establishments insignificant, since in their view those establishments have limited, respectively no direct or indirect contacts with other poultry, insignificant epidemiological role in recent HPAI epidemics, and they were relatively rarely infected (4 % of all outbreaks).

The authorities assert that backyard flocks are unlikely to contribute significantly to the spread of the virus. However, this assertion lacks strong support from epidemiological enquiries due to inherent limitations (as detailed in finding 65) and an incomplete epidemiological analysis (see also finding 56). The authorities had not consistently performed census within protection or surveillance zones around the outbreaks, and they could not demonstrate that those establishments were included in the screening activities, except for one instance in May 2023. Furthermore, five out of twelve infected non- registered establishments kept more than 100 birds (up to 235), prompting doubts about whether they played a similar epidemiological role as much smaller ones. These factors had not been considered in any formalised risk assessments. The absence of sufficient evidence supporting the insignificance of the risk of non-commercial establishments in HPAI epidemics is not in line with Article 85 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The TIR system does not contain information on the number of birds at each location. County authorities stated that many small-scale establishments registered in TIR had been inactive due to underreporting of a cessation of their activities. This is not in line with the provisions laid down in Articles 84, 93(a) and 101(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and in Article 18 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2035.

The local authorities organise their activities mainly based on the information provided by bird keepers prior each repopulation/re-stocking of establishments and the information provided by private veterinarians. However, these arrangements resulted in unnecessary delays of some official actions e.g., more than one week delay in a census of establishments located in the surveillance zone.

The shortcomings above had an impact on the application of control measures laid down in Regulation (EU) 2016/429 (Article 65) and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 3 (Chapters I and II of Part II) requiring the availability of accurate and updated inventories of poultry establishments in the event of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI to establish restricted zones, apply and regularly adapt those measures, and grant derogations therefrom.

Weaknesses in the registration of poultry establishments and the insufficient reliability of data prevent the authorities from having a properly updated information on the poultry establishments. The oversight of non-registered establishments raises concerns about the potential underreporting of suspicions in those flocks and their real role in the recent HPAI epidemics. This hinders the capacity of the competent authority to ensure the efficient application of the disease prevention, surveillance and control measures.

responses.response: the All flocks that pose a significant risk of avian influenza are registered in our system. Only backyard flocks kept for own onsumption are not registered. Although these flocks are at risk of disease emergence, as there is minimal or no animal, person and vehicle movement in these flocks, they do not play a role in disease spread. In recent years, around 5% of outbreaks have been detected in backyard flocks. In the recent epidemic started in autumn 2023, we have seen that in the settlements where the virus has appeared in backyard flocks, it has not appeared in commercial flocks. In addition, in those settlements where it appeared in both commercial and backyard flocks, in all cases it appeared in backyard flocks after the outbreak in commercial flocks; but in no case the appearance in backyard flocks resulted in a commercial outbreak. It is also clear that HPAI has not spread from a backyard outbreak to other flocks. Only one backyard flock was affected in each affected municipality. In no case was it confirmed that the disease had spread from the backyard flock. Therefore, it is still our opinion that the backyard flocks do not play a role in the spread of the disease and can

recommendations.text: To improve the effectiveness of the biosecurity measures applied by operators of poultry establishments, by evaluating their suitability to mitigate the prevailing risk factors involved in the areas where they are situated according to the local circumstances and practices. Thus, they will be able to prevent the introduction and minimise the spread of HPAI, in particular in areas with a high risk of incursion of the disease via migratory wild birds. Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4) and (5), and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. , and

citations.text: A model to estimate the risk of virus introduction in different areas of the country was completed by 31 March 2023. However, at the time of the audit, the experts that developed this model have not obtained yet complete population data for wild birds, nor the location of resting sites and migration1. Therefore, they were predicting new cases using a model that takes into account only the poultry population data, data on type of land/coverage, meteorological data and the previous outbreaks of poultry and wild birds. In addition, the authority and experts have plans to work on risk assessment for spreading of the infection between establishments, but the work has not started yet. The data that has not been incorporated into the risk assessment and the assessment that is still pending for the spread of the infection weakens the authority's endeavour to thoroughly effort to adequately identify all high risk-areas in the country.

The authorities named the main challenges they faced during recent epizootics: areas with high density of birds and poultry establishments, multiple birds movements (in particular waterfowl), airborne transmission of the virus, and inadequate biosecurity measures in establishments (e.g., inadequate disinfection of people and vehicles visiting establishments, sharing of staff and mechanisms). They have been trying to address some of those issues, (e.g., role of bird's catchers or vehicles from rendering plants, feed mills) 6 in spreading the disease by strengthening the measures applied to them. They also plan to introduce a wider monitoring of daily biosecurity operation on establishments by using live video feed, in particular during epidemics.

The fact that operators of many infected establishments did not comply with biosecurity rules is not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4)(b) and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on their responsibilities regarding disease prevention and knowledge and application of biosecurity measures. Completeness and updates of the Contingency plan

Risk assessment and identification of high-risk areas has allowed the competent authority to implement additional prevention, surveillance and control measures but this have not been sufficient to prevent the recurrence of epidemics waves. The inability of the authorities to reduce poultry density in areas proved problematic for epidemics will continue to challenge the veterinary service's capacity to deal timely with outbreaks.

The non-compliances on biosecurity, in particular in daily operational practices, contribute to an increased risk of the virus being introduced to poultry farms and would make it challenging to contain and control the spread of HPAI. The new compensation scheme for losses due to infection and wider engagement of poultry industry in biosecurity on commercial poultry establishments should contribute to improve compliance with biosecurity requirements.

Epidemiological investigations were generally done at the time of sampling or one or two days after. In the majority of instances, the local authority performed both the initial and final investigation. They used standardised form. In the initial inquiry they collected information on movements on and off suspected establishments during the incubation period (birds, vehicles, and personnel). However, in some cases, the official veterinarians did not include in the investigation report the likely origin of the infection or the full list of all contacts or had not followed these epidemiological links adequately due to lack of resources (e.g., links related to feed truck routes or establishments visited by the same team of birds catchers in incubation period). This is not in line with Articles 55(1)(g), 57 and 62 Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 8(3) and (4), of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. In their analysis the authority confirmed that such contacts contributed to spread of infection in the previous two epidemics (see also tables 3 and 4 in Annex II).

responses.response: Our central regulations on biosecurity and the requirements beyond legislation are professionally sound, so we do not see the need for major changes as they are still adequate. Some of ill our measures are transitional and some are specific to a articular area or time period. These are imposed, extended, atory modified or withdrawn according to the epidemiological situation. Our aim is not to formulate new disease control ion standards or principles, but to continuously review, refine and update our existing measures and encourage farmers to comply with these. . We will achieve this by: - Further tightening the compensation regulation to force farmers to comply with disease control rules. The technical discussions on the amendment of the legislation have been completed and are currently being negotiated between the ministries. - The central authority wants to reinforce the support and supervision it already provides to and over the regional authorities. In this context, it has concluded and is concluding contracts with specialised veterinarians with extensive epidemiological experience, who will carry out their duties both during epidemics and peacetime. They will be responsible fo

recommendations.text: To ensure the functionality of the contingency plans and the high level of disease awareness and preparedness in the counties, in particular those components identified previously (in Commission audits and lessons learnt) as weak point of their emergency response. Article 44 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. , and

citations.text: The simulation drills held aimed only at certain aspects of dealing with outbreaks and did not cover other essential components of emergency response (e.g., collection of 7 epidemiological data during epidemics, including enquiries, census and visits to establishments in the restricted areas). The authority had not verified the local authorities' preparedness for these tasks, or the ability to launch a rapid response. They missed an opportunity to share the experience gained in these areas during the previous period2. This is not in line with Article 44 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The fact that veterinarians are frequently dealing with HPAI epizootics might justify the lack of exercises but does not excuse the authorities of incorporating lessons learnt and measures to correct deficiencies which have been already identified during the previous two Commission audits. Currently, the authorities face the risk of continuing making the same mistakes in future epidemics unless they introduce the appropriate changes in their contingency plan, and unless they appropriate train the staff to follow the contingency plan. Early detection
The training and simulation exercises enhanced the knowledge of local authorities. But their limited scope prevented authorities to address some weaknesses identified in the recent HPAI epidemics.

citations.text: In 2021 and 2022 not all counties reached their targets for sampling of wild birds. A lower number of samples were noted also in two heavily affected counties in the South (which took less than 40% of their targets).

Since 2021 the authorities detected 73 outbreaks of HPAI in wild birds. However, 20 outbreaks were laboratory confirmed with more than one-week delay: in five instances with more than two weeks delay. At the time when the first few index outbreaks were detected in poultry, for which the authorities determined that introduction of the HPAI virus by wildlife was the most likely cause, the circulation of that HPAI virus had not yet been detected in wild birds in the affected areas. This undermines the effectiveness of the surveillance in wild birds and its role as early warning system and demonstrates inadequacy of the number and location of samples taken. citations.text: Since 2021 the authorities detected 73 outbreaks of HPAI in wild birds. However, 20 outbreaks were laboratory confirmed with more than one-week delay: in five instances with more than two weeks delay. At the time when the first few index outbreaks were detected in poultry, for which the authorities determined that introduction of the HPAI virus by wildlife was the most likely cause, the circulation of that HPAI virus had not yet been detected in wild birds in the affected areas. This undermines the effectiveness of the surveillance in wild birds and its role as early warning system and demonstrates inadequacy of the number and location of samples taken. That sub-optimal effectiveness of the early warning system in wild birds is not in line with provisions laid down in 2 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that although the gained experiences were not shared during the simulation exercises, the authority did this on other professional fora, like NDCC-LDCC and other meetings. 3 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that from 2020 an organization called "BirdLife Hungary" (the leading non-profit, apolitical, and charitable, nature conservation organisation in Hungary) and Hungarian National Parks are involved in the passive and ­ in the case of the former ­ also active surveillance of wild birds. This means that oropharyngeal/tracheal or cloacal swab samples are collected from live wild birds during bird-ringing. 8 Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Articles 3(1)(a) and (b)(i), 4(1)(b)(i) and 10(2) of, and Annex II to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/689.

In two establishments visited in high-risk counties, the audit team noted unnecessary delays in sampling (up to three days) for the laboratory confirmation of the disease. In one case, the private veterinarian decided to sample only for bacterial infection where symptoms compatible with HPAI were present. He only notified the suspicion for HPAI to the local authority once he got negative results for bacterial infection from the private laboratory. In the second case, the local authority had a positive laboratory result to a test made before authorising a movement. However, they decide to doubt the result since at that time, the birds did not show clinical signs; thus, they repeated sampling. This is not in line with Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 to ensure the timely detection of HPAI. Laboratory capacity- Diagnostics used for general early detection.

The laboratories are responsible for the transport of samples from the field to the laboratory in less than 24 hours. The audit team noted in the counties visited, that sometimes this deadline was not met and resulted in delays (for more see finding 64).

Although there is no evidence that the significant delays in confirming the infection in wild birds had a negative effect on the early detection of poultry outbreaks, these delays undermine the investigation of transmission pathways in poultry during the epidemics. 10

Unnecessary delays in the confirmation of outbreaks in domestic poultry through laboratory results resulted in delays in establishing control measures. This likely increased the risk of further spread of the disease and resulted in a higher number of infected establishments.

Since 2021, there were delays in providing laboratory results. On average, the turnaround time from suspicion to laboratory confirmation was two days. Out of 470 outbreaks detected since 2021, the official laboratories confirmed 173 outbreaks within one day. 193outbreaks (41%) were confirmed two days after suspicion and the laboratories needed three to seven days to confirm 104 outbreaks (22%). Delays in laboratory confirmation were noted also during the previous Commission audit and despite the commitments of 12 the authority to address them they failed to do it. In 26 outbreaks the authorities waited for laboratory confirmation before proceeding with culling. For the rest, the authorities started immediately with arrangements for the necessary control and eradication measures (e.g., depopulation and disposal); thus, they minimized a negative effect of these delays. In some other instances, those delays relate to preventive killing when the laboratory results were available only after depopulation.

Delays in confirmation of the disease, incomplete epidemiological enquiries, poor follow up of contacts with outbreaks, and inadequate screening and surveillance activities in restricted zones increased the risk of further uncontrolled spread of the infection. The authority partially mitigated these with the additional actions they applied, such as the extension of surveillance zones around the outbreaks and the strict actions applied on contact establishments.

recommendations.text: To make appropriate arrangements to perform adequate epidemiological enquiries and to follow up the epidemiological links identified so that the competent authorities can take appropriate preventive and control measures adapted to the causes and the risks of spread of the disease. citations.text: Epidemiological investigations were generally done at the time of sampling or one or two days after. In the majority of instances, the local authority performed both the initial and final investigation. They used standardised form. In the initial inquiry they collected information on movements on and off suspected establishments during the incubation period (birds, vehicles, and personnel). However, in some cases, the official veterinarians did not include in the investigation report the likely origin of the infection or the full list of all contacts or had not followed these epidemiological links adequately due to lack of resources (e.g., links related to feed truck routes or establishments visited by the same team of birds catchers in incubation period). This is not in line with Articles 55(1)(g), 57 and 62 Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 8(3) and (4), of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. In their analysis the authority confirmed that such contacts contributed to spread of infection in the previous two epidemics (see also tables 3 and 4 in Annex II).

Delays in confirmation of the disease, incomplete epidemiological enquiries, poor follow up of contacts with outbreaks, and inadequate screening and surveillance activities in restricted zones increased the risk of further uncontrolled spread of the infection. Articles 12(1)(a), 22(2), 26(1), 28(1),(5)(c), 41 and 43(1),(5)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. , and

citations.text: The authorities assert that backyard flocks are unlikely to contribute significantly to the spread of the virus. However, this assertion lacks strong support from epidemiological enquiries due to inherent limitations (as detailed in finding 65) and an incomplete epidemiological analysis (see also finding 56). The authorities had not consistently performed census within protection or surveillance zones around the outbreaks, and they could not demonstrate that those establishments were included in the screening activities, except for one instance in May 2023. Furthermore, five out of twelve infected non- registered establishments kept more than 100 birds (up to 235), prompting doubts about whether they played a similar epidemiological role as much smaller ones. These factors had not been considered in any formalised risk assessments. The absence of sufficient evidence supporting the insignificance of the risk of non-commercial establishments in HPAI epidemics is not in line with Article 85 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

During the epidemics, the central authority collected daily reports from the LDCCs which included updated information on outbreaks, e.g., epidemiological enquiries, depopulation, disposal of carcasses, compensation. Although the Department of Animal Health within the NFCSO includes trained epidemiologists, the epidemiological data available, e.g., incomplete epidemiological enquiries, had not allowed comprehensive analyses of the epidemiological situation, and thus, the NDCC could not appropriately use it to take informed and effective decisions. This is not in line with Article 43(2)(a), (c)(iii)(iv)(vi) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The experts from the NDCC visited the infected areas. During their on-site visits, they analysed the epidemiological situation and advised additional measures and modulation of actions, which were implemented. In doing so, they addressed, to some extent, the lack of sufficient crisis management tools that would enable them to conduct timely and more effective analyses. This deficiency in adequate tools had been previously identified in a Commission audit, but the authority has failed to address it.

At central level, the authority works on improvement of their mapping tool to make it fitter for epidemiological analysis and on finalising an IT tool (EPIDEMIR) that should serve for collecting epidemiological data from affected counties.

The county authorities pointed out that a mapping tool would help them to draw epidemiological maps during epidemics, to better understand the dynamics of the epidemic and to quickly collect and analyse the information available (e.g., on all 4 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted that the introduced methods are now accredited and have the certificate of compliance for proficiency test organised by the NRL. 11 registered poultry establishments located in restricted zones). Currently, they use a commercial product which is not customised for that purpose.

The local authorities were short of human resources, in particular during the peak of epidemics, for all task they needed to carry out. They prioritised some tasks, such as stamping out of outbreaks and granting movement derogations to reduce poultry density in the areas affected. They strengthened the LDCC in the most affected counties with additional staff coming from not affected areas. Due to their limited experience working with poultry and infections like HPAI, the seconded officials often conducted only certain tasks. The authorities did not carry out timely all activities they should have, and they did not implement quickly all the control measures necessary to contain the disease rapidly (e.g., depopulation of affected establishments and pre-emptive killing, official visits to poultry establishments in the restricted zones, completion of epidemiological enquiries). That was not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(c)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. The previous Commission audit detected similar deficiency for which the authority provided commitments to address it. However, their failed to implement them fully, which prevent those measures to work as expected in preventing recurrence of the disease.

The avian influenza expert group set up by the Chief Veterinary Officer held a full formal expert meeting in January 2019. Since then, there were regular meetings with some members of the expert group. The national avian influenza expert group was not adequately involved during the epidemics to support the competent authority in assessing all relevant measures for the control or eradication of the disease. This is not in line with Articles 43 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and 66 of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Dealing with suspect and confirmation cases. Restricted areas

The authorities did not identify and collect information of all non-commercial (backyard) poultry establishments within the restriction zones. This is not in line with Article 65(1)(a) 13 and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Articles 26 and 41 of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. The authorities confirmed that not all commercial establishments located in protection zone were inspected by official veterinarians. Instead of clinical inspections, they relied on passive surveillance and visited only those establishments that requested derogation for bird movements.

In the recent epidemics the authorities granted a total of 3,234 derogations for bird movements within and from restricted zones. The great majority (2,732) were direct movements from farms to slaughter. The remaining movements were granted for day-old chicks from hatcheries, in vast majority outside the restricted zone, and some movements of ready-to-lay poultry from or within restricted zones. The authorities did not grant any permission for introduction of birds from free area into restricted zones; instead, they accelerated the reduction of the population density in the restricted area.

The animal movements were carried out in line with most of the requirements, including clinical inspections, prior-movement testing for presence of HPAI virus, in sealed vehicles, on best available routes to avoid cross contamination, and they were all under official supervision. However, before granting a derogation from the measures applicable in a restricted zone, the authority did not take into account the local epidemiological situation, results of visits and their risk assessment was not sufficiently informative to ensure that the derogations would not endanger disease control. The competent authorities had mitigated this risk with compulsory prior-movement testing in which they detected additional 50 outbreaks. But the risk had not been negligible since some outbreaks were detected on establishments initially tested negative in prior-movement sampling but with HPAI virus detected in following days, i.e., some birds moved out been likely already infected. This is not in line with Article 28(1)(5)(c) and 43(1)(5)(c) of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. The authority only partially addressed the recommendation from the previous audit despite commitments and actions they provided to the Commission. Depopulation

Since the previous audit, the local authorities started to document their plans for killing birds during outbreaks, but those documents have been limited to essential information, e.g., number of birds to be killed, days for killing, order to transport company to provide vehicles for transport of carcasses and order to process carcasses in the rendering plant. The plans did not include certain details, e.g., staff available for activities related to killing, practical arrangements to ensure efficiency during killing, and further measures/actions to mitigate a risk of spreading of infection and prevent any unnecessary suffering of animals.

In one high-risk county, the authorities confirmed that no plans been prepared. Instead, the authorities relied on their experience from previous epidemics and their knowledge of the requirements. But as demonstrated on some outbreaks, the lack of detailed plan for killing resulted in unnecessary delays. The authority failed to satisfactory address identical deficiencies from the previous Commission audit despite the commitments provided. 14

The routine method of killing for large-scale establishments was sublimed dry ice. The authorities did not monitor the main parameters, i.e., temperature and carbon dioxide concentrations. The application of the method did not prevent directs contact of the animals with dry ice, which resulted in frostbites of unprotected bird's parts. Furthermore, the veterinarian met during the audit stated that in some instance the animals were rather dying from suffocation that due to CO2 effect. This is not in compliance with paragraphs 1 and 2 of Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009.

During recent epidemics, 41% of the outbreaks detected were depopulated three or more days after suspicion was reported; 22% at four or more days, 11% at five or more days and 5% more than 6 days up to two weeks. This delays, mainly due to lack of resources (personnel) occurred during the peak of epizootics, in particular around the holidays (Eastern, Christmas and New Year). This is not in line with Article 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Articles 12(1)(a) and 22(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Despite the commitments given to the Commission the authority had not satisfactory addressed the similar recommendation from the previous audit. Disposal and Cleaning and disinfection

The shortage of adequately trained staff, the lack of crisis management tools and the unreliability of data in existing databases undermine the effectiveness and efficiency of the actions taken to prevent and control the spread of HPAI, causing delays and requiring additional resources that could be otherwise assigned to other tasks.

The authority had not used the avian influenza expert group. This prevented the authority of getting expert advice, missing opportunities for improving their response strategy, improve their post-epidemic analysis and strengthen the prevention measures against HPAI recurrence.

Delays in confirmation of the disease, incomplete epidemiological enquiries, poor follow up of contacts with outbreaks, and inadequate screening and surveillance activities in restricted zones increased the risk of further uncontrolled spread of the infection. The authority partially mitigated these with the additional actions they applied, such as the extension of surveillance zones around the outbreaks and the strict actions applied on contact establishments.

The derogations granted for moving birds out of the restricted zones reduced the density of the poultry population and help to accelerate the eradication of the disease from those areas. However, the authorities did not adequately analyse the risk arising from these movements. The compulsory testing before animals were moved showed that some animals which were going to be moved were infected. Some although negative in testing originated from establishments with animals already in incubation period of the disease. 16 Thus, the movements might have contributed to spread the disease and make its control more challenging.

The authorities continued using dry ice as the main killing method during HPAI epidemics. The authorities did not address the deficiencies noted in the previous audit and the absence of appropriate procedures means that they do not safeguard the welfare of the animals and they inflict unnecessary suffering to them during killing.

The authority satisfactory addressed a shortage of disposal capacity noted in the previous audit, which helped to decrease the risk of spreading the disease after depopulation of establishments. However, the persistent delays in depopulating establishments resulted in an extended period keeping live infected animals, potentially shedding the virus. This situation facilitated the spread of the infection and led to some secondary outbreaks. The risk was only partially mitigated through preventive killing, as its application was also delayed due to resource constrains.

recommendations.text: To ensure that raw milk samples are taken from individual dairy holdings, as required by Chapter I.3.1 of Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, including holdings that deliver milk to milk collection centres.

citations.text: Joint MA-Ministry of Social and Labour Affairs Decree No 16/2008 on the testing of raw milk regulates the requirements for laboratory testing and control procedures for the placing on the market of raw milk of all animal species. However, the audit team noted that the Decree allows milk collection centres (MCCs) to test raw bulk milk for raw milk quality criteria instead of testing milk samples received from single dairy holdings, as required by Chapter I.3 of Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

National legislation and administrative measures covering the dairy sector have been enacted and are in line with relevant EU legislation, except for sampling and testing provisions in relation to the quality criteria of raw milk in collection centres. 3

In the MCC visited the FBO followed the requirements of Decree 16/2008 to test bulk milk in the MCC for PC/SCC and not milk of individual holdings. However, on the FBO's own initiative (and for the purpose of payment of raw milk based on quality) milk from individual holdings (delivering a quantity of raw milk ranging from 16 to 300 litres per day) was tested monthly for SCC (but not for PC).

The raw milk quality control system in place for SCC, PC and inhibitory substances is well established and enforced by the dairy industry and controlled adequately by the CAs, except for the sampling and testing of raw milk at MCC instead of at individual dairy holdings. This is not in line with the requirement of Chapter I.3 of Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

recommendations.text: To ensure that staff performing official controls and other official activities receive appropriate training for their area of competence, or that they receive additional training as necessary, to enable them to undertake their duties proficiently and to perform official controls and other official activities in a consistent manner, as required by Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: No specific training for the dairy sector has been provided in recent years as there have been no legislative changes in this sector. However, the findings regarding dairy inspectors' knowledge on HACCP-based procedures indicates there is a need for specific training on this topic (see paragraph 62).

Some weaknesses in relation to the technical knowledge of the CA staff were noted by the audit team during the official controls of the milk processing establishments, in particular 6 regarding the control over the FBOs' procedures in relation to pasteurisation of milk (see paragraphs 62, 65 and 66). Conclusions on competent authorities

The general training system in place, aimed at ensuring that official staff carry out their tasks adequately, does not include specific training on official controls in the dairy sector. No such training has been carried out in recent years. The official staff met was not fully knowledgeable in the technical matters pertaining to the dairy sector.
The insufficient competence/technical knowledge of official staff undermines the effectiveness of official controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls of food business operators' compliance regarding procedures based on HACCP principles, as laid down in Regulations (Nos) 852/2004, 853/2004 and 2073/2005, are effective as required by Article 8.1. of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: However, in one medium-sized establishment, the FBOs did not carry out sampling of five sampling units, as required by Article 5(1) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The 13 CGO officials responsible for the annual inspection stated that this deficiency had been noted and notified to the FBO. recommendations.text: To ensure the effectiveness, appropriateness, quality and consistency of official controls of the dairy sector through an adequate and effective supervision of the performance of the official staff, as required by Article 5(1) a) and b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: No audits were carried out in 2022 and 2023 to assess the effectiveness of official controls in the dairy sector.

Supervision of DGO official staff performance is the responsibility of the CGOs. However, the audit team noted that there is no established procedure for such supervision: in some CGOs this is limited to the evaluation of the percentage of completion of the control plan (without investigating their effectiveness), whilst, in others, some either observe inspections or carry out follow-up inspections to evaluate the performance of DGO and/or CGO staff. The results of these supervisory exercises, however, were not recorded. Conclusions on system of supervision and internal audits

Internal audits are carried out as planned. However, the performance of official controls in the dairy sector has not been targeted in these audits and supervisory mechanisms to evaluate staff performance are not standardised and are seldom recorded.

audits.title: evaluate controls on residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products

recommendations.text: To ensure that the residue control plans are implemented fully in line with pertinent EU requirements (in terms of requisite minimum sampling frequencies) and planned arrangements. Relevant EU legislation: Annexes I and II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1646, and Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/932.

citations.text: BACKGROUND 4.1. Legal framework for controls on residues in animals and food of animal origin Member States are legally obliged to implement control plans for residues of pharmacologically active substances in animals and animal products (3). These comprise three plans: a national risk-based control plan for production in the Member States, a national randomised surveillance plan for production in the Member States, and a national risk-based control plan for third-country imports into the EU. These plans are subject to annual Commission evaluation (4). Member States must establish multiannual national control programmes for pesticides residues (5) in food and feed of both animal and non-animal origin and they must also participate in the Union-wide coordinated multiannual programme (6). Member States must control the presence of certain contaminants in food of both animal and non-animal origin ((i) in food placed on the Union market, and (ii) in food of animal origin entering the Union). The foodstuffs of animal origin to be tested and the categories of contaminants to be tested are specified (7) as is the sampling frequency (8). These control plans are also subject to annual Commission evaluation (9). The scope of this report is limited to the competent authorities' implementation of control plans for residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products. It does not cover the controls on residues in food and feed of non-animal origin.

As was the case for the NRCP samples in finding 4, the implementation of the NRSP plan did not fully meet the requirements (37) with respect to the minimum sampling frequencies in 2023 and 2024, with 58% and 77% taken respectively of the total minimum requirement of 165 samples. The audit team noted that samples for the NRSP were taken across the calendar year, however with similar reductions in certain months to that seen for the NRCP in finding 2. 5.3. Implementation of the multiannual national control programme for pesticide residues and the Union-wide coordinated multiannual programme

In 2023, 425 samples were planned, and 304 samples were tested giving an overall achievement rate of 72% (43). In 2024, 510 samples were planned and 396 were tested, giving an overall achievement rate of 78%.

In the 2023 contaminants plans, 373 of the 421 samples planned for all commodities, excluding processed products of animal origin, were tested giving an achievement rate of 89%. For processed products of animal origin in 2023, 40 samples were planned and 293 were tested (43). In 2024, 599 of 752 samples planned were tested across all commodities, an overall achievement rate of 80%.

Achievement rates for the controls on contaminants in food of animal origin in 2023 and 2024 did not meet the minimum requirements for sample numbers analysed (49) for certain commodities, as summarised in the table below. While the basis for the operation of control and surveillance plans is in place for residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants, incomplete implementation of the sampling plans in 2023 and 2024, in addition to shortcomings in the supervision of implementation of sampling, undermine the overall effectiveness of the residue control plans.

recommendations.text: To ensure that actions taken in case of non-compliances, in particular when illegal treatment is established, are fully aligned with pertinent requirements of EU legislation. Relevant EU legislation: Articles 3-6 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2090, and Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The national procedure allows that if a product has already been manufactured from non-compliant raw material, the competent authority "can decide on the fate of the manufactured product on the basis of a risk assessment, taking into account the test results", which contradicts pertinent EU requirements (51).

The OV is to evaluate the results and decide on the measure(s) to be taken in case of non-compliant result(s). The OVs interviewed by the audit team stated that they had not received any training on the topic and experienced difficulties to refer to applicable EU requirements, including on measures in case of suspected or confirmed illegal treatment (52), and when residues were identified at concentrations below the maximum residue limits for pharmacologically active substances authorised in veterinary medicinal products or as feed additives but where the presence of those residues was inconsistent with the food chain information (53).

The audit team scrutinised the follow-up of four non-compliant results for pharmacologically active substances and one for pesticides, and observed the following: · In one case (where illegal treatment was established), the competent authority did not take samples from all relevant batches belonging to the farm, and no (50) Articles 3, 4 and 5 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2090. (51) Bullet point 1 of Article 5(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2090. (52) Article 6 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2090. (53) Article 4(2) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2090. 14 regular additional official controls were performed, which is not in line with relevant legal requirements (54). · In another example, a non-compliant result, due to interpretation error, was identified 10 months after the issuing of the analysis report. Furthermore, the NFCSO, while being informed by the laboratory of the non-compliant result at the time of issuing the analysis report, did not notice that the investigation report had not been received within the 30 days required by the national procedure (55). · For another non-compliant sample reviewed, the auditors noted that the analysis result was reported 3 months after the sampling took place (target turnaround time being 30 days), thus impacting the effectiveness of the measures taken. Conclusion on follow-up and enforcement

While there is a system in place to deal with non-compliant results, the actions taken are not fully aligned with pertinent EU legal requirements which undermines the overall effectiveness of the residue control system. 5.6. Laboratories, methods of analysis, method validation, and quality control 39. During 2023-2024, the laboratory network consisted of four national laboratories, all of which were within the NFCSO organisation. The audit team visited two laboratories, one with predominant responsibility for testing of the plans relating to pharmacologically active substances and some contaminants and the other with responsibility for testing of the plans relating to pesticides and contaminants.

audits.title: To evaluate the implementation of actions taken by the Hungarian authorities to address recommendations of audit report DG(SANTE)/2021-7205 - animal by-products (ABP) and derived products (DP)

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when assessing the operator's compliance, either when granting approval for ABP processing plants or during official controls, the operator meets all of the infrastructure and equipment requirements for a plant and, in particular, has put in place appropriate own checks and HACCP-based proce- dures, including the results of operators' own checks and validation of the pro- cessing plant.

audits.title: evaluate the authorisation and controls of marketing and use of Plant Protection Products

recommendations.text: To ensure that when outsourcing evaluations for authorisation of plant protection products, the fees and charges are established in a transparent manner and there are measures in place to make certain that the assessment of applications for authorisation of plant protection products is independent, objective and transparent. This is to comply with Articles 36(1) and 74(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, read in conjunction with Article 29(b)(iii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: NÉBIH relies on the clause in the cooperation agreements that the companies `shall ensure the availability of personnel with the necessary qualifications and appropriate 5 experience'. It is not aware of and does not verify the qualifications and competence of the experts used by the companies for the evaluations.

An accredited company will only be involved in the evaluation of PPP authorisations if the applicant requests it in the application and specifies which of the two companies he has selected. If the competent authority accepts the request, the applicant will then enter into a contractual agreement with the company for the work and pay for it. Thus, it is not the competent authority that contracts the actual evaluation work or pays for it; in the cooperation agreement with NÉBIH, it is specifically stated that `the evaluation body shall carry out its evaluation activities in accordance with this cooperation agreement with NÉBIH without any financial compensation'. NÉBIH is not privy to the contract or the financial arrangements between the applicant and the company.

The competent authority has the final say in the evaluations and remains the authority for the subsequent authorisation. Nevertheless, the audit team considered that the arrangement of a direct financial agreement between the applicant and the evaluating company is not transparent. Article 74(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 requires that fees or charges are established in a transparent manner. Furthermore, the arrangement does not protect against potential influence on the outcome of the evaluation due to the payment made and to the lack of an effective mechanism against possible conflict of interest, even if there are examples in practice of the evaluating company making negative proposals. Article 36(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 requires that assessments are independent, objective and transparent, and Article 29(b)(iii) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 requires that delegated bodies are impartial and free from any conflict of interest. General authorisation procedure

There is a procedure for authorisation of PPPs to ensure proper handling of applications. However, for a number of the authorisations, the evaluation is outsourced to private companies in a way that is not in line with EU legislation. The financial arrangements and the lack of an effective mechanism for managing conflicts of interest do not protect against potential influence on the outcome of the evaluation. In spite of this outsourcing of work, there are still significant delays in the authorisation process, which are a non- compliance.

recommendations.text: To ensure that emergency authorisations are issued and reported in line with Article 53(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, in particular that: a) the scope addresses only one danger b) the validity period for each authorisation does not exceed 120 days c) each authorisation is reported immediately to the European Commission and other Member States and includes all the required information 20 d) for active substances that are approved in the EU, authorisation mechanisms other than repeated emergency authorisations should be promoted e) continued authorisation of kasugamycin should be reconsidered in view of one-health policy and risks of possible antimicrobial resista is

citations.text: Since 2017, the annual number of emergency authorisations granted in Hungary has been in the range of 20-30. Each year, there have been several authorisations for the same 7 active substance, but for different commercial products. On the other hand, some authorisations were for a wide range of crops and pests, such as the one for a PPP containing the active substance kasugamycin mentioned in paragraph 24 below, which is not in line with Article 53(1) of Regulation (EC) 1107/2009, which stipulates that an emergency authorisation is for `a danger', i.e. not a broad range of different dangers. Furthermore, while each notification to the EU database indicated no more than the maximum of 120 days allowed, the actual granted period of use, across the range of crops could be longer. For example, the audit team noted that for several diquat products, the authorisations and product labels stated first use (e.g. for winter oilseed rape) 26 May 2025 and last use (e.g. for sunflower) 31 October 2025, resulting in a total period of use of 158 days. Another example is the 2025 kasugamycin product authorisation, which across the various crops covers a period from 30 April to 28 September, i.e. a period of 151 days. The audit team also noted that most of the emergency authorisations were not reported to the EU database before they entered into force, but with a delay of up to a couple of months. Thus, relevant requirements in Article 53(1) of Regulation (EC) 1107/2009 are not complied with. Furthermore, not all details were provided in the reporting, e.g. no indication was made when it was a repeated authorisation, and no information generally provided under the fields `8. Area permitted to be treated', `9. Area actually treated' or `10. Further limitations'.

For several active substances, PPP emergency authorisations have been issued repeatedly for 6, 7 or 8 years. The audit team noted that at least some of these applications, where the active substances are approved in the EU, would be more correctly accommodated, at least over time, within the conventional authorisation framework maintaining the system's integrity as referred to in `Commission Staff Working Document on emergency situations according to Article 53 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009'. Penoxulam (a herbicide) is the approved active substance with the most repeated PPP emergency authorisations (8 years in a row). The authorisations have included use in sorghum and rice. NÉBIH noted that an extension to minor use in sorghum was made. There are furthermore alternative authorised PPPs available for rice. There may therefore no longer be a need for emergency authorisations for PPPs with that active substance in those crops.

The audit team also noted that for 7 years in a row, an emergency authorisation was given for a PPP containing the active substance kasugamycin (an antibiotic) for use in pome fruit against fire blight (Erwinia amylovora) and in vegetable crops for various other bacterial diseases in outdoor and indoor production. NÉBIH stated that a risk assessment for antimicrobial resistance had been carried out. Nevertheless, the audit team had concerns about these authorisations from a one-health policy point of view. The EU withdrew the approval of this active substance in 2005, and according to the EU database, no other Member State has authorised its use in the last 10 years. Conclusions on authorisation of PPPs 8

Emergency authorisations are overall granted in line with documented procedures. However, they are often granted for wide groups of crops and pests and for longer periods than 120 days, which is not in line with Article 53 of Regulation No (EC) 1107/2009.

The emergency authorisations often also involve approved active substances. The dangers which these authorisations are addressing could therefore, at least over time, be contained by obtaining PPP authorisations as per Articles 33, 40, or 51 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Using emergency authorisations repeatedly instead, waters down the integrity of the authorisation system.

Most emergency authorisations are not communicated immediately to the Commission and other Member States, and many are notified incorrectly or incompletely. In view of the risk of creating antimicrobial resistance, the audit team had some concerns about the repeated authorisations of kasugamycin.

recommendations.text: To ensure that when planning inspections at users of plant protection products, the results of the monitoring of water status under programmes referred to in Article 8 of Directive 2000/60/EC are taken into account, as required by Article 24(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation is based upon conclusion No 53

citations.text: For planning the controls, the results of the programmes for the monitoring of water status are not taken into account, which is not in line with Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. But the results of the pesticide monitoring programme, which is implemented by NÉBIH itself, is taken into account in the way that non-compliances found regarding maximum residue levels or unauthorised PPPs are followed up by inspections. E.g., an exceedance of the pesticide maximum residue level was identified in the monitoring programme at the vegetable grower visited by the audit team (see paragraph 80 below). This had been followed up in a previous inspection.

recommendations.text: To ensure that in the official controls, samples of plant protection products are analysed to determine the presence of unacceptable co-formulants as referred to in Article 27 of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and the content of impurities subject to conditions and restrictions under Article 6(b) of the same Regulation. Such controls are required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Laboratory's PPP formulation analysis focuses on the active substances and on the physical properties. Its scope does not extend to unacceptable co-formulants or regulated impurities. This is not in line with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on laboratories used for formulation analysis of PPPs
The laboratory testing does not include analysis for unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities, which reduces the value of the sampling programme.

recommendations.text: To ensure that during controls of imports, manufacture or repacking of plant protection products, it is verified that products destined for other Member States are authorised in those Member States. This is to comply with Article 28(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. For consignments that are Customs cleared during import controls, notification should also be made to the Member State of destination to enable that Member State to comply with Article 28(1) of the same regulatio

citations.text: Although the inspections observed were overall effective and carried out competently, some flaws were noted by the audit team: · At the retailer, packets with a PPP containing acetamiprid had an outdated label. Next to them on the shelf was a pile of papers with the updated label text, so that for each 15 sale, the customer would be given a copy of the updated text together with the wrongly labelled PPP. This was considered acceptable in the inspection, even if the authorisation for the product stipulates that an additional, self-adhesive label must be placed on the package. · For PPPs destined for other Member States at the manufacturer and the packer, Customs controls do provide some guarantees that those PPPs leave Hungary and are not marketed there. However, there were no checks that those PPPs were authorised in the Member State of destination. This does not ensure full compliance with Article 28(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Import controls

Customs identify consignments of PPPs from the tariff codes and refer them to the plant health inspectors, who then carry out documentary and physical checks. This is done for 100% of the PPP consignments. The checks include verification that the active substance is approved in the EU. PPP or active substance imports do not require prior notification from the importer or pre-approval from the CA. Nevertheless, the integrity of each import is checked by verifying the batch numbers with the authorisation holder. For that purpose, the border control post has a list of contacts that are available 24 hours a day. This procedure is also followed for PPPs destined for or in transit to other Member States. However, it is not verified that the PPP is authorised in the receiving Member State. This does not ensure full compliance with Article 28(1) and (2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. Furthermore, notification is not made to the receiving Member State if a consignment, customs cleared in Hungary, is on the way, which limits the possibilities of that Member State to ensure that the mentioned Articles are complied with.

Official controls at production and marketing level are comprehensive and overall carried out well. However, for manufacturers and packers, it is not verified that PPPs destined for other Member States are authorised there.

Import controls of PPPs intended for use in Hungary and other Member States are in place and largely carried out satisfactorily. However, for imports destined for other Member States, it is not verified that the PPPs are authorised there.
